title: Foundation for Virtual and Augmented Reality Systems

course_goals.text: Analyze the foundational concepts, historical evolution, and human sensory factors governing Extended Reality systems.
Understand the technical architecture of XR systems, including hardware components, tracking mechanisms, and software development principles.
Apply systematic design and implementation methodologies to develop, evaluate, and refine interactive XR systems.
Explain and apply advanced techniques for managing computational resources, optimizing rendering, and solving complex navigation problems in immersive environments.
Implement and develop basic Extended Reality applications using industry-standard platforms.

concepts.name: Extended reality
concepts.definition: Extended reality (XR) refers to extending reality by some means. Systematically, it involves using systems to either augment our reality or replace our perception of reality.

concepts.name: Virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is the extreme end of the reality-virtuality continuum where the user's perception of the real world is completely replaced by a simulated environment.

concepts.name: Augmented reality
concepts.definition: Augmented reality is an extended reality concept that exists on the reality-virtuality continuum. These concepts fall between the complete replacement of reality (Virtual Reality) and the entirely real world.

concepts.name: Mixed reality
concepts.definition: Mixed reality is the broad space between the completely real and completely virtual environments, encompassing various degrees of augmentation.

concepts.name: Immersive technology
concepts.definition: Immersive technologies are a type of technology where a user's senses are blocked, transporting them into a virtual world. These technologies are used across various application domains.

concepts.name: Reality-virtuality continuum
concepts.definition: Reality-virtuality continuum is a scale used to visualize the spectrum between a completely real environment and a completely virtual environment.

concepts.name: Virtual environment
concepts.definition: Virtual environment is one extreme of the scale where there is nothing real present, meaning the environment is completely virtual.

concepts.name: Augmented virtuality
concepts.definition: Augmented virtuality is the opposite of augmented reality, where a virtual world is enhanced by incorporating real-world content.

concepts.name: Metaverse
concepts.definition: The Metaverse is not merely an application of virtual reality, mixed reality, or augmented reality technology. The Metaverse is a broad concept that involves reimagining how humans interact with the digital world in an all-around 3D environment.

concepts.name: Human-computer interaction
concepts.definition: Human-computer interaction is a discipline focused on the design, evaluation, and implementation of interactive computing systems for human use. It also involves the study of major phenomena that surround the development of these systems.

concepts.name: Cognitive side
concepts.definition: Cognitive side refers to the understanding of the human mind that is necessary to grasp how our senses influence the desired experience when using technology or a system.

concepts.name: Psychological side
concepts.definition: Psychological side refers to the understanding of the human mind that is necessary to grasp how our senses influence the desired experience when using technology or a system.

concepts.name: Interactions
concepts.definition: Interactions refers to the process of designing and implementing how users engage with the environment within VR or AR systems.

concepts.name: Virtual tours
concepts.definition: Virtual tours are experiences that allow a user to visit a place remotely, even if they cannot physically go there. This method saves both money and physical effort for the user.

concepts.name: Heritage tourism
concepts.definition: Heritage tourism involves allowing users to explore a heritage place virtually, even if physical visits are restricted. This enables users to explore every part of the heritage space without having to travel there.

concepts.name: Preservation of digital heritage
concepts.definition: Preservation of digital heritage is the process of digitally saving a heritage space, often in the form of virtual tours. This digital preservation can increase the lifespan and potential for the space to be visited by many users.

concepts.name: Non-immersive
concepts.definition: Non-immersive systems are virtual experiences obtained through a computer-generated environment where the user controls activities, but the environment does not directly interact with the user. These systems rely on psychological engagement, meaning the user is mentally absorbed in the virtual world while remaining physically attached to the real world.

concepts.name: Augmentation
concepts.definition: Augmentation is the process of enhancing the real world by overlaying digital content onto it. This focus is distinct from Virtual Reality, which emphasizes a fully simulated environment.

concepts.name: Immersive experience
concepts.definition: Immersive experience is the generation of stimuli designed to stimulate all of the user's sensory organs. This experience can be partly immersive, as seen in 3D movies, even if it is not fully immersive.

concepts.name: Virtual tape measure
concepts.definition: Virtual tape measure is an augmented reality application that allows users to measure heights or lengths of objects. This tool eliminates the need for carrying a physical tape measure.

concepts.name: Markerless AR application
concepts.definition: Markerless AR application is a versatile type of AR that does not require placing any markers in the physical world. These applications function based on computer vision techniques, allowing users to decide where virtual objects are placed.

concepts.name: Marker-based
concepts.definition: Marker-based systems utilize specific markers and simple algorithms for development. Although these systems are easier to create, they require a highly controlled environment because the markers are susceptible to damage in outdoor settings.

concepts.name: Markerless
concepts.definition: Markerless techniques are used to overcome the maintenance difficulties of markers. These techniques primarily rely on computer vision and may utilize other sensors, such as GPS sensors, for location-based applications.

concepts.name: Artificial environment
concepts.definition: Artificial environment is a computer-generated setting that is not real, which must be populated with artificial objects. This environment can be a graphical representation of either a real world or an imaginary world.

concepts.name: Sensory stimuli
concepts.definition: Sensory stimuli are computer-generated inputs that a VR system provides to the user. These stimuli allow the user to experience the artificial or synthetic environment through their sensory organs, such as their eyes and ears.

concepts.name: Interactivity
concepts.definition: Interactivity is the characteristic of a VR system where dynamic changes in the virtual environment occur based on the user's actions or inputs. This allows the user to interact with the elements present in the environment, similar to how they interact with objects in the real world.

concepts.name: Superimposition
concepts.definition: Superimposition is a category of AR system where extra information is placed over the building space. This allows digital content to appear on the real-world view.

concepts.name: Phases
concepts.definition: Phases are distinct periods into which the evolution of the field can be divided, although some overlap may occur between them.

concepts.name: Stereoscopic device
concepts.definition: Stereoscopic device is a type of apparatus that allows the brain to interpret two-dimensional images as three-dimensional objects. This device established the possibility of creating a sense of depth from flat images.

concepts.name: Stereoscopic vision
concepts.definition: Stereoscopic vision is the biological ability of the brain to perceive three-dimensional space by viewing two-dimensional images. This perception allows us to see images together as objects existing in 3D space.

concepts.name: Head-mounted display
concepts.definition: Head-mounted display is a new kind of computer display that people began working on in the 1950s. It is a device worn by the user to display visual information.

concepts.name: Haptic feedback
concepts.definition: Haptic feedback is a method where touch sensations are provided to the user. This allows the user to feel objects on the screen while manipulating them.

concepts.name: CAVE system
concepts.definition: CAVE system is a type of immersive environment that used a single computer to render images in a surrounding setting, giving the user the sensation of being surrounded by holograms.

concepts.name: WTK package
concepts.definition: WTK package is a software package developed in 1992 that provided higher-level tools for application development within Virtual Reality (VR).

concepts.name: Virtual Reality Modeling Language
concepts.definition: VRML (Virtual Reality Modeling Language) is a modeling language for VR that was presented in 1994, appearing alongside other modeling languages such as X3D and Java 3D.

concepts.name: Field of view
concepts.definition: Field of view is the extent to which the user's field of vision is captured by the display in a VR headset. A larger field of view generally results in greater immersion.

concepts.name: Growth phase
concepts.definition: Growth phase is the last and continuing phase of VR evolution, which began around 2016. This phase is characterized by continuous development and acceleration of the field.

concepts.name: Experimental phase
concepts.definition: Experimental phase is the initial period of development that occurred before the 1980s. This phase was primarily related to early experimentation, which defined concepts and showed the types of technology required.

concepts.name: Tools or applications phase
concepts.definition: Tools or applications phase is the period spanning from the mid-1990s to 2007. During this phase, early applications and exploratory tasks were developed, focusing on interaction techniques, usability, and design theory related to AR.

concepts.name: Commercial application phase
concepts.definition: Commercial application phase is the current phase, starting from 2007. This phase is characterized by widespread AR availability and the continuous emergence of newer applications in various market domains.

concepts.name: Tracking
concepts.definition: Tracking is a technology used to register content in three dimensions, enabling augmented reality overlays on real-world markers or providing outdoor interfaces through GPS tracking.

concepts.name: Computer-generated imagery
concepts.definition: Computer-generated imagery is graphics created by a computer that can appear either superimposed over the real world view or as a substitute for the real world view. This imagery is used to augment or replace the user's perception.

concepts.name: Prototype AR system
concepts.definition: Prototype AR system is an early functional system that combined an optical see-through head mounted display with a ceiling-mounted mechanical tracking system and custom graphics hardware. This system was designed to register 3D content based on head movements.

concepts.name: AR interaction methods
concepts.definition: AR interaction methods refer to the ways in which a user can interact with the augmented digital content. Work was carried out on these methods in 1993.

concepts.name: Viewpoint tracking
concepts.definition: Viewpoint tracking is a significant challenge in AR that involves developing systems, such as computer vision tracking based on printed matrices or markers, to accurately register content in 3D space.

concepts.name: Wearable computing
concepts.definition: Wearable computing refers to devices, such as headsets, where the computer hardware is carried externally, for example in a backpack. Interaction with these devices is achieved through different input devices.

concepts.name: AR overlay on real-world marker
concepts.definition: AR overlay on real-world marker is a technique that uses computer vision to place augmented reality content onto physical markers in the real world.

concepts.name: Commercial phase
concepts.definition: Commercial phase is the stage of AR evolution where AR experiences transition from niche research to becoming widely popular and available to the general public. This phase is characterized by increased commercial interest and the potential for AR applications to drive sales and popularity of goods.

concepts.name: AR authoring tools
concepts.definition: AR authoring tools are software that enable the creation of Augmented Reality experiences. These tools, such as those based on Adobe Flash, made it possible to experience AR directly through web browsers, thus expanding accessibility.

concepts.name: ARKit SDK
concepts.definition: ARKit SDK is a Software Development Kit launched by Apple for the purpose of developing Augmented Reality systems. This launch significantly stimulated growth in the field by allowing a large number of developers to create AR applications.

concepts.name: Defining characteristic
concepts.definition: Defining characteristics are features that help distinguish between different types of systems. These characteristics allow one to differentiate between a virtual reality system and an augmented reality system, for example.

concepts.name: Virtual reality system
concepts.definition: Virtual reality system is an artificial environment that is experienced through sensory stimuli. This environment is provided by a computer and allows the user's actions to partially determine what happens within it.

concepts.name: Technological issue
concepts.definition: Technological issue refers to the engineering challenge of generating suitable sensory stimuli required for a user to experience a virtual or artificial environment. This issue focuses on the creation of the inputs, distinguishing it from the psychological challenge of how the user perceives those stimuli.

concepts.name: Psychological issue
concepts.definition: Psychological issue refers to the challenge of how a user perceives the stimuli that have been generated. This relates to the human factor and how individual psychological characteristics affect perception.

concepts.name: Immersion
concepts.definition: Immersion is the objective or technological experience provided by a system. Immersion aids the potential for a user to feel present in a virtual world.

concepts.name: Extensive
concepts.definition: Extensive refers to the range of sensory modalities that are presented to the user. The more sensory organs that are stimulated by the stimuli provided by the computer, the more extensive the immersion is.

concepts.name: Matching
concepts.definition: Matching refers to the congruence between different sensory modalities. For instance, the visual presentation must instantly correspond to head motion and the virtual representation of the user's body.

concepts.name: Surrounding
concepts.definition: Surrounding is the extent to which the cues provided are panoramic. This refers to the scope of the field of view for visual senses or the extent of auditory perception for sound sources.

concepts.name: Vivid
concepts.definition: Vivid is the quality of energy stimulated within a particular sensory modality. This quality relates to how much energy the computer generates to stimulate a sensory organ, which is enhanced by factors such as resolution, lighting, and audio bitrate.

concepts.name: Presence
concepts.definition: Presence is the subjective experience of feeling truly located within a virtual world. Presence is achieved when a user is unable to distinguish between the real world and the virtual world.

concepts.name: Representational fidelity
concepts.definition: Representational fidelity is the degree to which the VR experience conveys a place that is or could be on Earth. This fidelity measures how closely the VR experience matches or exploits the familiarity of a real-world place.

concepts.name: Experiential fidelity
concepts.definition: Experiential fidelity is the degree to which the user's personal experience matches the intended experience of the VR creator. Higher experiential fidelity is achieved when real-world constraints are incorporated into the virtual world's navigation, movement, and interaction.

concepts.name: Immersion
concepts.definition: Immersion is a major concept in Virtual Reality systems that is tied to the technological aspects and issues of the experience. This concept is distinct from presence, which addresses the psychological concerns of the user.

concepts.name: Pose
concepts.definition: Pose refers to the viewer's position and orientation within the context of the system. Pose determination is necessary to register virtual content in the real world.

concepts.name: Registration phase
concepts.definition: Registration phase determines the pose of a viewer relative to a real world anchor. This phase is performed when the user begins using the system.

concepts.name: Tracking phase
concepts.definition: Tracking phase is the process that follows registration, requiring the continuous updating of the viewer's pose relative to a previously known pose. This is necessary because the user is likely to move while using the AR application.

concepts.name: Real world anchor
concepts.definition: Real world anchor is a reference point in the real world used by the system to determine the viewer's pose, which includes position and orientation. This determination is necessary to register virtual content accurately so that it appears seamlessly within the physical environment.

concepts.name: Uncanny valley effect
concepts.definition: The uncanny valley effect is a phenomenon where making environments familiar to the user can sometimes lead to feelings of uneasiness or creepiness. This occurs even when the objective is to make the environment as familiar as possible to the user's real-world experience.

concepts.name: Cyber sickness
concepts.definition: Cyber sickness is a condition that may result from a mismatch between the user's physical motion and the virtual motion. This sickness increases based on the duration of exposure and other factors.

concepts.name: Mitigation
concepts.definition: Mitigation refers to the strategies that can be adopted to overcome the challenges associated with cybersickness. Finding a feasible solution to reduce the impact of cybersickness is extremely important in the context of VR systems.

concepts.name: Motion sickness susceptibility
concepts.definition: Motion sickness susceptibility is an internal factor referring to an individual's tendency to experience motion sickness, which is often correlated with increased risk of cyber sickness. Individuals with higher susceptibility are likely to experience more severe cyber sickness symptoms when immersed in realistic virtual reality environments.

concepts.name: Body awareness
concepts.definition: Body awareness is the ability of the user to attend to and perceive bodily sensations. This awareness can be affected by factors such as poor sleep quality.

concepts.name: Inter-pupillary distance
concepts.definition: Inter-pupillary distance (IPD) is the distance between the user's pupils. This distance determines how stereoscopic vision is achieved through the HMDs.

concepts.name: Latency
concepts.definition: Latency is the time gap between an action performed in the physical world and the corresponding change reflected in the virtual world. Increased latency is found to increase the likelihood of inducing sickness.

concepts.name: Latency jitter
concepts.definition: Latency jitter is the variability in the time gap between a user's action and its reflection in the virtual world. This variability causes irregularities in the timing of data delivery, leading to discomfort and disorientation.

concepts.name: Type of display
concepts.definition: Type of display is a hardware factor that significantly influences the severity of cybersickness symptoms. Users utilizing Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs) tend to feel more cyber sick compared to those using conventional monitors.

concepts.name: Type of input
concepts.definition: Type of input refers to the various methods used in virtual reality, such as hand controllers or treadmills. The specific input device or technology used can cause cybersickness to vary.

concepts.name: Visual motion
concepts.definition: Visual motion stimulus is the movement experienced by the user within a virtual environment. This stimulus is considered one of the primary causes of cyber sickness, and its severity is affected by how the content moves.

concepts.name: Vection
concepts.definition: Vection is the sensation of self-motion, which is the feeling of movement experienced by the user. This sensation is highest when the user perceives motion in peripheral stimuli.

concepts.name: Means of locomotion
concepts.definition: Means of locomotion refers to how a user is moving within the virtual world. This aspect of movement affects cyber sickness because a mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause disorientation.

concepts.name: Questionnaire-based input
concepts.definition: Questionnaire-based input is a method of input where users rate their discomfort or disorientation using self-report scales. These scales are typically administered before, during, or after the experience.

concepts.name: Physiological input
concepts.definition: Physiological input is an objective method used to detect cybersickness by measuring bodily functions. Examples of these inputs include heart rate, galvanic skin response, and EEG.

concepts.name: Behavioral input
concepts.definition: Behavioral input involves detecting cybersickness using observable cues related to how a user moves. These cues include head and body movement, blink rate, and postural sway.

concepts.name: Content-based input
concepts.definition: Content-based input measures cybersickness by analyzing features within the virtual reality environment itself. These features include optical flow and depth cues.

concepts.name: Simulator Sickness Questionnaire
concepts.definition: Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is one of the most extensively used questionnaires for measuring cybersickness. Although originally designed for non-VR purposes, it was adapted for the VR context and contains 16 items divided into three subscales: oculomotor, disorientation, and nausea.

concepts.name: Manual evaluation
concepts.definition: Manual evaluation is a measurement technique that relies on human intervention to assess cyber sickness. This process requires someone to distribute questionnaires, collect feedback, and analyze responses to determine the severity or onset of cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Automated evaluation
concepts.definition: Automated evaluation is a measurement technique that uses automated algorithms to measure cyber sickness. This method processes various inputs, such as physiological or biometric data, to automatically determine the presence of cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Transparent models
concepts.definition: Transparent models are types of models that provide clear insight into their internal workings and decision-making process. When an automated evaluation uses these models, the process is easily understood.

concepts.name: Stepwise regression analysis
concepts.definition: Stepwise regression analysis is a method utilized to measure cyber sickness using a variety of physiological signals. This technique is considered to be a transparent model.

concepts.name: Cybersickness
concepts.definition: Combined system is the combination of engineered and natural lenses. This dual system essentially helps the user perceive the immersive visual content.

concepts.name: Questionnaire-based subjective input
concepts.definition: Questionnaire-based subjective input is a type of input collected by using questionnaires to gather subjective data.

concepts.name: Mitigation strategies
concepts.definition: Mitigation strategies are methods, implemented by either the developer or the user, designed to reduce the negative effects of cybersickness. These strategies aim to lessen the severity of the symptoms.

concepts.name: Interpretable model
concepts.definition: Interpretable models are similar to transparent models and offer flexibility in how they are used. Interpretable models provide precise details regarding the relationship between the input provided and the output received.

concepts.name: Black box model
concepts.definition: Black box models are types of models whose decision-making process is shrouded in mystery and cannot be easily understood. The model simply takes input and produces an output, making the relationship between them difficult to discern.

concepts.name: Hybrid model
concepts.definition: Hybrid models are combinations of different machine learning algorithms designed to leverage the strengths of various approaches. These models aim to achieve both high predictive accuracy and a degree of transparency in their decision-making process.

concepts.name: Prediction
concepts.definition: Prediction is the ability to anticipate upcoming Cybersickness (CS) incidents before they happen, allowing for potential mitigation measures.

concepts.name: Detection
concepts.definition: Detection is the process of identifying Cybersickness (CS) after the experience has already taken place, meaning the input is generated after the experience.

concepts.name: Classification labels
concepts.definition: Classification labels are an output from machine learning-based evaluation that indicates the likelihood or severity of Cybersickness (CS).

concepts.name: Sickness score
concepts.definition: Sickness score is a numerical value that quantifies the severity of the Cybersickness (CS) experience.

concepts.name: Self-report questionnaire
concepts.definition: Self-report questionnaire is a tool used to gather data for Cybersickness (CS) evaluation, providing users with rating scales to provide scores.

concepts.name: Developer's perspective
concepts.definition: The developer's perspective is the way developers view the problem and how they can address it. This involves determining what the developers can do to solve the issue.

concepts.name: User's perspective
concepts.definition: The user's perspective involves what users can do to prevent cyber sickness. This highlights that proper usage is necessary even if a good solution is provided.

concepts.name: Symmetric mask
concepts.definition: Symmetric mask is a classical approach that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity.

concepts.name: Ground visible restrictor
concepts.definition: Ground visible restrictor is a technique that ensures the ground plane remains visible during movement.

concepts.name: Dynamic visual blur
concepts.definition: Dynamic visual blur is a technique that reduces the possibility of cyber sickness by obscuring or reducing the clarity of the visual environment. This technique can be implemented using two types of blur effects.

concepts.name: Depth of field blur
concepts.definition: Depth of field blur is a type of visual blur effect that utilizes well-known depth cues found in human vision. This effect is one of the two types of dynamic visual blur.

concepts.name: Rest frame
concepts.definition: Rest frame is a fixed element within the virtual environment that remains stationary relative to the real world, regardless of the user's movements. These frames are used as a technique to reduce cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Optical flow manipulation
concepts.definition: Optical flow manipulation is a technique that involves visually mixing optical flow patterns in the reverse direction of the virtual visual motion. This manipulation aims to reduce the perceived optical flow.

concepts.name: Sparse peripheral display
concepts.definition: Sparse peripheral display is a hardware addition that expands the periphery of a Head-Mounted Display (HMD) using a colorful LED matrix. This modification is used to reduce the effects of cybersickness.

concepts.name: Phantom legs
concepts.definition: Phantom legs is a technique that uses additional hardware to apply alternating haptic cues synchronized with the user's footsteps. This method was found to manage to reduce cybersickness to a great extent.

concepts.name: Floor vibrations
concepts.definition: Floor vibrations is a technique that utilizes vibration-driven whole body tactile feedback. It attempts to match the vibrations that occur in the virtual environment.

concepts.name: Modified motion platform
concepts.definition: Modified motion platform is a piece of hardware that can be adjusted to reduce cybersickness. Short bursts of rotational acceleration can be used to match the visual forward acceleration to achieve this effect.

concepts.name: Viewpoint snapping
concepts.definition: Viewpoint snapping is a modification to the locomotion technique that renders moving pictures in discrete chunks during rotation. Such methods are novel approaches to manipulating movement in a virtual world to potentially reduce cybersickness.

concepts.name: Habituation
concepts.definition: Habituation is a process where the intensity of cyber sickness gradually decreases after a person experiences the virtual environment repeatedly. This gradual reduction in symptoms is achieved through repeated exposure.

concepts.name: Internal
concepts.definition: Internal causes are subjective factors that relate to a user's personal characteristics, such as age or gender. These factors are inherent to the individual experiencing the symptoms.

concepts.name: External
concepts.definition: External causes are related to the physical components or the content being presented. These issues can stem from either the hardware or the content itself.

concepts.name: Evaluation strategies
concepts.definition: Evaluation strategies are methods used to measure cybersickness, involving inputs, a process (which can be manual or automated), and outputs like classes or numerical values. These strategies help quantify the severity of the sickness.

concepts.name: VR hardware
concepts.definition: VR hardware refers to the physical components, such as computers, headsets, and controllers, that are used to create the VR experience. These components are part of the overall VR setup.

concepts.name: Stimulation
concepts.definition: Stimulation is the data flow generated by the VR hardware that produces sensory input designed to override the user's natural senses. This process is the mechanism by which the hardware interacts with the organism component of the overall VR system.

concepts.name: Surrounding physical world
concepts.definition: The surrounding physical world is the real-world environment that must be considered part of the VR system. This is necessary because the user may respond to stimuli, such as light or sound, coming from this real environment.

concepts.name: Head tracking
concepts.definition: Head tracking is the most critical type of tracking commonly utilized in Virtual Reality (VR). It monitors the movement of the user's head.

concepts.name: Display or output device
concepts.definition: Display or output device is any device that produces output to stimulate a user's sensory organs. This term is used broadly and does not require the device to be a visual display.

concepts.name: Sensor or input device
concepts.definition: Sensor or input device refers to any tracking device that captures user input. Sensors are devices that extract information from the real world, specifically tracking user movements.

concepts.name: Computer or processing part
concepts.definition: Computer or processing part is a device that processes inputs and produces outputs. This element allows the user to perceive the virtual world.

concepts.name: World grounded devices
concepts.definition: World grounded devices are input devices that are fixed in the real world and do not move. These devices are often used to interact with grounded desktop or systems.

concepts.name: Non-tracked handheld controllers
concepts.definition: Non-tracked handheld controllers are devices held in the hand but are not tracked in 3D space by the system. Because they are not tracked, the system does not know the controller's exact position relative to a reference frame.

concepts.name: Bend sensing gloves
concepts.definition: Bend sensing gloves are a type of data glove that detects hand postures and gestures because sensors are placed at all bend positions or joints. The processing unit receives continuous raw data from these sensors to detect the gesture.

concepts.name: Bare hand inputs
concepts.definition: Bare hand inputs are interactions where the system tracks the bare hand using computer vision techniques. This allows users to provide gestures without needing to wear or use any external device.

concepts.name: Non-hand-based input device
concepts.definition: Non-hand-based input device captures input from parts of the body other than the hand, such as head movement, eye gaze, or voice. These devices allow the system to capture input from various parts of the user's body.

concepts.name: Head tracking based input device
concepts.definition: Head tracking based input device uses the user's head motion for input, detecting movement along axes like yaw, roll, and pitch. This detection allows the device to infer the kind of input and change the view accordingly.

concepts.name: Eye tracker
concepts.definition: Eye tracker devices typically come integrated with headsets and are used to track how the user's eyes are moving. The system uses this tracking data to infer what to do and accordingly takes necessary action.

concepts.name: Midas touch problem
concepts.definition: Midas touch problem is a difficulty in eye tracking where the system cannot differentiate whether a user's gaze is intentional for selection or merely a natural, purposeless blank gaze. This inability can cause the system to select objects when the user did not intend to.

concepts.name: Multimodal input
concepts.definition: Multimodal input is a preferred method of interaction that utilizes multiple forms of input. This approach works better than relying solely on eye tracking-based input.

concepts.name: Full-body tracking
concepts.definition: Full-body tracking is a non-hand input method that tracks movement of more than just the head and hands. This tracking adds to the illusion of self-embodiment and social presence in the virtual world because the user sees a fuller representation of themselves.

concepts.name: Motion capture suit
concepts.definition: Motion capture suit (MOCAP) is an approach to full-body tracking that utilizes a suit containing various sensors. These sensors capture and transmit raw movement data from different parts of the body, which is then converted into full body position and movement.

concepts.name: Camera-based tracking
concepts.definition: Camera-based tracking is an input method that uses multiple surrounding cameras to detect movement. The system infers the overall body movement of a character by detecting the movement of fiducial markers worn by the actor.

concepts.name: Sound tracking
concepts.definition: Sound tracking is a non-hand input technique that captures voice, speech, and non-speech sound. This input is captured using devices like microphones or microphone arrays for interaction within the virtual world.

concepts.name: Inertial measurement unit
concepts.definition: Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) is a composite hardware containing three types of sensors, which is a popular group of sensors often found in modern head-mounted displays.

concepts.name: Computer
concepts.definition: Computer is a device that processes data coming from input sensors and then activates or actuates the output devices. This processing is central to the function of the VR system.

concepts.name: Graphics Processing Unit
concepts.definition: Graphics Processing Unit is a specialized processor typically used to speed up the rendering process. This speed is achieved because of its inherent ability to perform parallel processing.

concepts.name: Middleware
concepts.definition: Middleware is a layer that can exist between the developer and the hardware, allowing developers to follow well-known patterns and avoid handling complicated micro-level details.

concepts.name: Visual display
concepts.definition: Visual display is a device designed to stimulate the user's visual sense, which is the sense of sight. These displays are used to render the experience in virtual and augmented reality.

concepts.name: Head-mounted displays
concepts.definition: Head-mounted displays (HMDs) are wearable and mobile pieces of equipment that integrate electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components. HMDs place images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens.

concepts.name: World-fixed displays
concepts.definition: World-fixed displays are stationary display surfaces that render graphics onto surfaces that do not move with the user's head. These displays range from standard monitors to large screens that completely surround the user.

concepts.name: Regular displays
concepts.definition: Regular displays are mobile or stationary devices, such as tablets or smartphones. These displays are typically relevant for non-immersive virtual reality and are often used for augmented reality.

concepts.name: Haptics
concepts.definition: Haptics are outputs that explore the sense of touch perception, and they can be categorized based on various criteria. These outputs are used to provide physical feedback in virtual environments.

concepts.name: Passive device
concepts.definition: Passive device is a static physical object that is not controlled by the computer, allowing users to feel interaction with virtual objects. These devices match the shape of the virtual objects in the real world.

concepts.name: Active device
concepts.definition: Active device is a physical object that provides feedback and is controlled by the computer to give a sense of touch when dealing with virtual objects. These devices are used to simulate touch in virtual experiences.

concepts.name: Tactile sensation
concepts.definition: Tactile sensation refers to touch perceptions obtained through the activation of the skin. Unlike proprioceptive forces, which activate joints or muscles, tactile sensations are generated directly on the skin surface.

concepts.name: Proprioceptive force
concepts.definition: Proprioceptive force is a type of sensation that activates the user's joints or muscles. This force provides a sense of limb movement and muscular resistance.

concepts.name: Motion platform
concepts.definition: Motion platform is a hardware device that moves the entire body, resulting in a sense of physical motion and gravity, while conveying orientation, vibration, acceleration, and jerks.

concepts.name: Active motion platform
concepts.definition: Active motion platform is a type of motion platform that is controlled by computer simulation, meaning the computer controls the platform's movement.

concepts.name: Passive motion platform
concepts.definition: Passive motion platform is a type of motion platform that is controlled by the user, and therefore has no direct computer control.

concepts.name: Treadmill
concepts.definition: Treadmill is an output device that provides the sensation of walking or running while the user remains in one place by providing different sorts of input to the feet or legs.

concepts.name: Omnidirectional treadmill
concepts.definition: Omnidirectional treadmill is an output device that provides the sensation of walking or running while the user remains stationary. These systems can be active, utilizing computer-controlled mechanical parts, or passive, where the user controls the movement themselves.

concepts.name: Headsets and glasses
concepts.definition: Headsets and glasses are a category of augmented reality devices used to provide AR experiences. Examples of this category include AR HoloLens and Google Glass.

concepts.name: Handheld devices
concepts.definition: Handheld devices are a category of augmented reality hardware that includes devices such as smartphones and tablets. These devices can be used for various applications like e-commerce and tourism.

concepts.name: Projection-based systems
concepts.definition: Projection-based systems are augmented reality devices that utilize methods like interactive projectors and AR sandboxes. These systems are used in fields such as industrial design and medical training.

concepts.name: Head-up displays
concepts.definition: Head-up displays are a type of AR hardware that is typically found in vehicles. These displays can be integrated into gaming experiences, medicine, and sports.

concepts.name: Spatial AR
concepts.definition: Spatial AR is an augmented reality system where digital content is overlaid onto a physical environment. This type of system is characterized by its ability to support multi-user engagement, allowing several users to interact with the augmented content simultaneously.

concepts.name: High-definition hologram
concepts.definition: High-definition hologram is the digital content that is integrated with the real-world view. This content is projected onto the user's view, allowing the digital information to appear in the physical environment.

concepts.name: Smart glasses
concepts.definition: Smart glasses are a category of AR devices that are typically lighter and resemble standard eyeglasses. They are used for AR application deployment but are less immersive than Head-Mounted Displays.

concepts.name: Marker-based AR
concepts.definition: Marker-based AR is a type of augmented reality where specific markers are placed in the real world. The system recognizes these markers using image recognition to augment specific content.

concepts.name: Spatial AR device
concepts.definition: Spatial AR device is a type of augmented reality where digital content is overlaid onto specific physical objects, rather than being overlaid onto the user's view of the real world. The defining feature is that the display element is independent of the user.

concepts.name: Room-scale AR
concepts.definition: Room-scale AR is a specific type of augmented reality where devices typically use projectors to display graphical information directly onto physical objects. This contrasts with other AR types where content is overlaid on the user's view.

concepts.name: Interactive display
concepts.definition: Interactive display is a surface that is converted into a display by projecting images onto it, allowing users to interact with the projected content.

concepts.name: AR contact lens
concepts.definition: An AR contact lens is a future wearable device that superimposes digital images or information directly onto the wearer's field of vision via the lens. These lenses are very small and can be placed directly on the eye like a regular contact lens.

concepts.name: Headsets
concepts.definition: Headsets are a type of wearable AR hardware. They are characterized as older technology and an older concept when compared to modern glasses.

concepts.name: Glasses
concepts.definition: Glasses are a modern, state-of-the-art wearable AR device that is rapidly advancing in development.

concepts.name: Sensing
concepts.definition: Sensing is the lowest level of the process, where sense organs are stimulated by a particular type of stimuli. These organs then convert that input stimuli into neural impulses.

concepts.name: Sense organ tracking
concepts.definition: Sense organ tracking involves tracking the user's sense organs, such as eyes and ears, whose degrees of freedom are controlled by the body. This tracking is necessary so that the position and orientation of the organ can be reflected in the virtual world.

concepts.name: Other body part tracking
concepts.definition: Other body part tracking monitors non-sense organ body parts, such as hands or facial expressions, to reproduce the user's body in the virtual world. This tracking can range from continuous movement to simple input signals, like pressing a button, to change a predetermined body configuration.

concepts.name: Environment tracking
concepts.definition: Environment tracking involves tracking physical objects in the real world that surround the user. This is crucial in augmented reality (AR) to properly register digital content in 3D, and in virtual reality (VR) to prevent physical harm.

concepts.name: Outside-in tracking
concepts.definition: Outside-in tracking is a method where the trackers or sensors are part of the environment, rather than being part of the devices the user is wearing or using.

concepts.name: Inside-out tracking
concepts.definition: Inside-out tracking is a method where the tracker carries the sensors that are integrated into the devices the user is wearing or using.

concepts.name: Calibration
concepts.definition: Calibration is the phase where the tracker is oriented as close to the real world as possible.

concepts.name: Registration
concepts.definition: Registration is the step used to estimate or determine the starting position and orientation of the sensor. Knowing this initial location is necessary before tracking movement can begin.

concepts.name: Integration
concepts.definition: Integration is the step where sensory measurements are aggregated at specific, discrete points in time. This process combines data from multiple sensors to effectively track the target object or environment.

concepts.name: Drift correction
concepts.definition: Drift correction is the phase that compensates for the mismatch between the estimated position and orientation and the actual values. This process aims to reduce the error in the tracking estimation.

concepts.name: Inside-out
concepts.definition: Inside-out refers to a tracker where all the necessary sensors are placed directly onto the device that the user is utilizing.

concepts.name: Outside-in
concepts.definition: Outside-in refers to a tracker that utilizes sensors placed within the surrounding environment, rather than placing them on the user's device.

concepts.name: Gyroscope
concepts.definition: Gyroscope is a sensor that captures the angular velocity of movement.

concepts.name: Accelerometer
concepts.definition: Accelerometer is a sensor that captures the linear acceleration along the three axes: x, y, and z.

concepts.name: Magnetometer
concepts.definition: Magnetometer is a sensor that captures the magnetic field strength along the three axes.

concepts.name: Measurement error
concepts.definition: Measurement error is the difference between the measured value from a sensor and the actual, ideal value. This difference occurs because sensors are imperfect devices.

concepts.name: Sum of squared errors
concepts.definition: Sum of squared errors is a method used to compare data from two sensor types by computing the difference between corresponding values, squaring that difference, and then summing all the resulting squared values across all samples.

concepts.name: Linear least squares
concepts.definition: Linear least squares is a classical regression problem used to optimize a function by minimizing the square term of the difference between the predicted and actual values.

concepts.name: Initial orientation
concepts.definition: Initial orientation is the direction the headset is facing when the tracking system is first turned on. This setting establishes the forward direction for the initial alignment.

concepts.name: Angular velocity sample
concepts.definition: Angular velocity sample is the sample of angular velocity obtained from the gyroscopic sensor at a specific instant. This sample indicates the rotation or change in orientation.

concepts.name: Gain parameter
concepts.definition: Gain parameter is a normalized value between 0 and 1 used in drift correction. This parameter is applied to combine the separately estimated orientation at a specific time instant.

concepts.name: Electromechanical tracker
concepts.definition: Electromechanical tracker consists of a serial or parallel kinematic structure composed of links that are interconnected using joints and equipped with sensors. These trackers are used to capture movement data in virtual and augmented reality environments.

concepts.name: World-fixed electromechanical tracker
concepts.definition: World-fixed electromechanical tracker is a type of electromechanical tracker that is stationary and fixed in a specific environment. This setup typically includes a display, mechanical pivoting, and tracking sensors attached to the entire structure.

concepts.name: Wearable tracker
concepts.definition: Wearable tracker is a type of electromechanical tracker that is designed to be worn directly on the body of the user. These trackers capture real human movements which are then translated into virtual world movements.

concepts.name: Avatar
concepts.definition: Avatar is an animated representation of a real human being that is created using wearable trackers. The movements of the human wearing the tracker are tracked and translated to the avatar's movement in the virtual world.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic tracker
concepts.definition: Electromagnetic tracker is a non-contact position measurement device that tracks movement by using a magnetic field generated by a stationary transmitter. This field determines the real-time position of a moving receiver element.

concepts.name: Acoustic tracking
concepts.definition: Acoustic tracking is a method of tracking that utilizes ultrasonic signals to determine the real-time position of a moving object. This technique is also referred to as ultrasonic tracking.

concepts.name: Line of sight
concepts.definition: Line of sight is a requirement for acoustic tracking, meaning the transmitter and receiver must be able to communicate without any obstacle positioned between them.

concepts.name: Vision-based tracker
concepts.definition: Vision-based tracker is a type of tracker that determines poses, such as position and orientation, using optical sensors or cameras. These trackers are currently very prevalent in the field.

concepts.name: Optical sensor
concepts.definition: Optical sensor is a device that determines poses by using optical means, such as cameras. These sensors are categorized into infrared, visible light, and 3D structure types.

concepts.name: Infrared tracking
concepts.definition: Infrared tracking is a vision-based sensing technique that utilizes infrared sensors and targets that emit or reflect light. This approach is robust to adverse illumination effects, such as poor ambient lighting or harsh shadows.

concepts.name: Outside looking in
concepts.definition: Outside looking in is a tracking method where targets are attached to the object being tracked, but the cameras are placed externally in the environment. The cameras detect the targets and use this information to determine the object's pose and position.

concepts.name: Visible light tracking
concepts.definition: Visible light tracking is a method that utilizes visible light sensors or optical cameras to perform tracking. These sensors are commonly found in consumer-grade electronic devices and wearable devices.

concepts.name: Fiducial tracking
concepts.definition: Fiducial tracking is a method that uses artificial landmarks added to the environment to aid in registration and tracking. These artificial landmarks allow the system to track specific objects or areas within the environment.

concepts.name: Natural feature tracking
concepts.definition: Natural feature tracking registers camera pose in real time using features that are already present in the natural environment. This process requires advanced image processing algorithms to detect unique features such as points, corners, and line intersections.

concepts.name: Model-based tracking
concepts.definition: Model-based tracking is a visible light sensing category that involves techniques for mapping and localization within a real environment. This technique is often used to simultaneously create and update a map while tracking positions.

concepts.name: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping
concepts.definition: Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) is a technique that simultaneously creates and updates a map of the real environment while localizing positions within it. This technique was originally developed for robot navigation and has since been adapted for augmented reality.

concepts.name: 3D structure tracking
concepts.definition: 3D structure tracking is a technique that involves creating 3D models of the structures present in the environment and using those models for the augmentation of the real-world view.

concepts.name: 3D model
concepts.definition: 3D models are digital representations of objects created using software like Autodesk Maya, which are utilized to build the immersive experience.

concepts.name: 3D structure sensing
concepts.definition: 3D structure sensing is the process of creating 3D models of the structures present in an environment. These models are then utilized for the augmentation of the real-world view.

concepts.name: Inertial tracker
concepts.definition: Inertial tracker is a self-contained sensor that measures changes in an object's orientation, translation velocity, or acceleration. These trackers are typically based on microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and have no range limitations.

concepts.name: Real Time Kinematic technology
concepts.definition: Real Time Kinematic technology (RTK) is an enhancement to basic GPS that uses GPS signal carrier waves for measurement. This technology provides greater accuracy compared to a basic GPS system.

concepts.name: Motion capture
concepts.definition: Motion capture is the technique of digitally recording movements of real things, usually humans. This technique can be based on any tracking method.

concepts.name: Eye-tracking system
concepts.definition: Eye-tracking system is a type of tracker that can be incorporated into other trackers. Such a system typically tracks the gaze point or area of the gaze of the user.

concepts.name: Hybrid tracker
concepts.definition: A hybrid tracker is a tracking method that utilizes two or more basic tracking systems. This combination of systems is employed to achieve the tracking goal.

concepts.name: VR software
concepts.definition: VR software is the type of software used in the context of Virtual Reality (VR) or Augmented Reality (AR). VR software must drive the hardware to generate a VR experience by utilizing the user's senses.

concepts.name: Input device
concepts.definition: Input devices are utilized by the user to perform an operation that generates data. This generated data is then sent into the VR system for processing.

concepts.name: Output device
concepts.definition: Output devices are responsible for generating suitable stimuli. These stimuli are intended to affect the user's sense organs.

concepts.name: Rendering
concepts.definition: Rendering is the process of creating the stereoscopic view, which serves as the output of the VR experience. This term is used broadly and can refer to stimulation of senses other than the visual sense.

concepts.name: Software Development Kit
concepts.definition: Software Development Kit (SDK) is a tool utilized for specific headsets that manages low-level operations such as device drivers, head tracking, and display output.

concepts.name: Platform
concepts.definition: Platform is a broader term than headset, referring to a specific combination of hardware and operating system.

concepts.name: Game engine
concepts.definition: Game engine is a type of middleware specifically created or adapted for generating VR experiences, though it was originally developed for building any type of game.

concepts.name: Virtual world generator
concepts.definition: Virtual world generator is an abstraction of the entire software system that converts input information into output so that the experience appears real to the user. It is responsible for maintaining the internal reality of the virtual environment.

concepts.name: Internal reality
concepts.definition: Internal reality is the state that the Virtual world generator maintains so that the virtual experience appears real to the user. This maintained reality allows renderers to extract necessary information to calculate outputs for the displays.

concepts.name: Input events
concepts.definition: Input events are data that arrive from low-level systems, such as a head tracker or game controller, and are arranged in a queue for systematic processing by the software.

concepts.name: Virtual world
concepts.definition: Virtual world is a visual scene that may appear real or be synthetically created. When synthetic, it requires defining numerous triangles in a 3D space, essentially a triangular mesh.

concepts.name: Triangular mesh
concepts.definition: Triangular mesh is a structure created by defining numerous triangles in a 3D space, which is required to create a synthetic scene.

concepts.name: Computer graphics
concepts.definition: Computer graphics addresses computer-generated images that are derived from synthetic models. The software used to build an application must support these computer graphics operations.

concepts.name: Texture mapping
concepts.definition: Texture mapping is an operation where camera images taken of a real object are mapped onto a synthetic object within the virtual world. This is a common operation in computer graphics.

concepts.name: Material properties
concepts.definition: Material properties are the physical characteristics of surfaces that indicate how they interact with elements such as light, sound, and forces. These properties must be maintained alongside the geometric mesh.

concepts.name: Matched motion
concepts.definition: Matched motion is the correspondence between user motions in the real world and the virtual world. This ensures that the virtual environment accurately reflects the user's physical movements.

concepts.name: Matched zone
concepts.definition: Matched zone is a specific area where the real and virtual worlds perfectly align. Within this zone, the user can move physically in the real world, and that movement is translated to the virtual world.

concepts.name: Locomotion
concepts.definition: Locomotion is the act of moving oneself within the virtual world when the user's physical motion is not matched in the real world. This allows users to explore virtual environments without making corresponding physical movements.

concepts.name: Mismatch of obstacles
concepts.definition: Mismatch of obstacles occurs when there is a discrepancy between physical and virtual barriers in the matched zone. This happens when a user can be blocked by a virtual obstacle but not a physical one, or vice versa.

concepts.name: User locomotion
concepts.definition: User locomotion is a concern regarding how a user moves themselves within the virtual world. Support for user locomotion is important to address potential sickness issues.

concepts.name: Avatar
concepts.definition: Avatar is the representation of the user in the virtual world. This avatar can perform activities like walking, running, or swimming without the user needing to move physically.

concepts.name: Vehicle metaphor
concepts.definition: Vehicle metaphor is a route planning technique used to simulate movement between points. It allows the user to experience travel along a fixed route as if they were sitting in a moving vehicle.

concepts.name: Physics support
concepts.definition: Physics support is a required feature that ensures the virtual world behaves like the real world by governing how objects move and interacting with physical phenomena. This support includes replicating how light, sound, and smell propagate through the environment.

concepts.name: Collision detection algorithm
concepts.definition: Collision detection algorithm determines whether two or more bodies are intersecting in the virtual world. This process is distinct from collision response, which dictates the appropriate behavior of the intersecting bodies after detection.

concepts.name: Collision response
concepts.definition: Collision response is the appropriate action needed after a collision takes place. This response determines how objects should react when they intersect with other objects.

concepts.name: Basic laws of mechanics
concepts.definition: Basic laws of mechanics are the fundamental rules that govern how objects move in the virtual world, ensuring that the virtual environment behaves similarly to the real world. Support for these laws is considered sufficient for basic functionality, distinguishing them from advanced laws which are used to increase realism.

concepts.name: Shared virtual world
concepts.definition: Shared virtual world is a collaborative VR experience created over a network and maintained by a system or server. Each user within this environment is assigned a distinct matched zone.

concepts.name: Matched zone
concepts.definition: Matched zone is a distinct area assigned to each user within a shared virtual world. These zones may overlap in the real world or be disjoint and distributed globally.

concepts.name: Physics
concepts.definition: Physics, in the context of a virtual world, refers to the algorithms that govern how objects behave within the environment. This includes handling movement, detecting collisions, and determining the response to those collisions.

concepts.name: Game engine
concepts.definition: Game engine is a middleware that sits between the hardware and higher-level application software, abstracting hardware functionalities for developers of Extended Reality (XR) applications.

concepts.name: Rendering engine
concepts.definition: Rendering engine is a component designed to help generate animated 3D graphics by utilizing various methods.

concepts.name: Audio engine
concepts.definition: Audio engine consists of algorithms related to loading, modifying, and generating sound through a speaker system.

concepts.name: Physics engine
concepts.definition: Physics engine is a crucial component responsible for emulating the laws of physics within an application.

concepts.name: Rasterization
concepts.definition: Rasterization is a rendering technique used to generate animated 3D graphics. Compared to ray tracing, rasterization is less computationally intensive.

concepts.name: Native application
concepts.definition: Native application is a type of deployment that requires the use of Software Development Kits (SDKs) specifically tailored to the platform and hardware.

concepts.name: Web deployment
concepts.definition: Web deployment refers to the method of deploying systems so that they can be accessed and run over the web.

concepts.name: Augmented reality software (AR Software)
concepts.definition: Augmented reality software is the specific set of tools and programs used for implementing augmented reality. This technology area is being discussed alongside virtual reality.

concepts.name: Low-level software libraries
concepts.definition: Low-level software libraries are tools that require considerable skill from the developer. Developers must possess skill in both understanding the library functions and in coding to call those functions.

concepts.name: Standalone AR authoring tools
concepts.definition: Standalone AR authoring tools are types of software designed for novice users or developers. These tools assume that the user does not require any programming skill to operate them.

concepts.name: Framework
concepts.definition: Framework is a combination of multiple libraries created to facilitate Augmented Reality system development. This combination allows developers to overcome the limitations of single, low-level toolkits.

concepts.name: Low-level library
concepts.definition: Low-level libraries provide access to the core tracking and display functionality necessary to build an Augmented Reality application. These libraries require strong programming ability from the developer.

concepts.name: Scene graph
concepts.definition: Scene graph represents computer graphic scenes as a node-based graph. This structure allows the entire scene to be represented as a tree, enabling selective manipulation and realistic effects.

concepts.name: 3D registration
concepts.definition: 3D registration is the process of creating and rendering a three-dimensional object at a specific position in the real world. This operation is necessary after the system has recognized a marker or feature.

concepts.name: Rapid prototyping and development tools
concepts.definition: Rapid prototyping and development tools are software used to quickly visualize or create prototypes of an idea before committing to major coding efforts. These tools allow users to test ideas simply rather than going through the entire coding exercise.

concepts.name: Authoring tool
concepts.definition: An authoring tool is a popular software used for creating prototypes that include multimedia content for web and desktop platforms. These tools allow the creation of a variety of desktop and mobile experiences.

concepts.name: AR toolkit
concepts.definition: An AR toolkit is a version of an Augmented Reality (AR) toolkit that has been ported over to a specific platform, such as Flash. This toolkit enables users to have an AR experience directly from within their web browser.

concepts.name: 3D registering
concepts.definition: 3D registering is the activity of loading and overlaying virtual content onto the tracked image. The FLAR Toolkit implements this activity alongside tracking.

concepts.name: Rapid prototyping tools
concepts.definition: Rapid prototyping tools are specialized tools used to quickly create an initial version of an Augmented Reality application, allowing developers to continue work on various categories of AR software.

concepts.name: Open Frameworks
concepts.definition: Open Frameworks is an open-source C++ middleware library that functions as a combination of multiple libraries, designed to support interactive experiences on both desktop and mobile platforms.

concepts.name: Client device
concepts.definition: A client device, in the context of AR architecture, is primarily treated as a rendering device or a client that connects back to a backend server for content provision and computation.

concepts.name: Low-level libraries and frameworks
concepts.definition: Low-level libraries and frameworks are tools that require the highest level of programming skill when dealing with AR software. These are situated at one extreme of the spectrum of required programming ability.

concepts.name: Plugin
concepts.definition: Plugins require a basic authoring tool to function, and AR support is provided through this add-on software. Plugins do not come as a complete package but rely on an existing basic software to provide AR functionality.

concepts.name: Content authoring tool
concepts.definition: A content authoring tool is a software application that allows a user to create interactive 2D or 3D content. This tool is the base software that plugins are added to.

concepts.name: Interactive 3D graphics authoring tool
concepts.definition: Interactive 3D graphics authoring tools are programs used to create interactive 3D applications, such as Unity or Vizard. Most of these tools include plugins specifically for AR visualization.

concepts.name: Plugin-based approach
concepts.definition: Plugin-based approach utilizes specialized plugins, such as Vuforia, within larger authoring tools like Unity to provide an easy and quick method for developing AR applications. However, the support provided by the underlying authoring tool can limit the developer's flexibility in deciding on different interaction methods or interface look and feel.

concepts.name: Low-level software development tool
concepts.definition: Low-level software development tools are used to build a custom system from scratch rather than depending on a third-party tool. This method is employed to resolve the issues and cons associated with high-level authoring tools.

concepts.name: Standalone authoring tool
concepts.definition: Standalone authoring tools are software that require the least amount of programming skill when working with AR software. These tools represent the opposite extreme of the programming skill requirement spectrum.

concepts.name: Graphical user interface
concepts.definition: Graphical user interface (GUI) is a visual interface, often drag-and-drop type, that developers use to create an application or experience. This interface allows users to create an experience without requiring coding.

concepts.name: Human factors
concepts.definition: Human Factors refers to the knowledge that helps a developer build better Extended Reality systems by understanding the factors relevant to the user experience. This knowledge is crucial for designing effective XR systems.

concepts.name: Ubiquitous computing
concepts.definition: Ubiquitous computing is a state where users can access multiple connected computers that communicate with each other, allowing the user to operate them without separate intervention.

concepts.name: Layman user
concepts.definition: Layman user is a person who uses a system without being a technology expert, focusing only on using the system rather than understanding its internal workings.

concepts.name: Lay person
concepts.definition: A lay person is an end user who is not necessarily an expert in the technology behind the system. Designers of interactive systems should cater to these users without forcing them to learn complex technical details.

concepts.name: Technical jargon
concepts.definition: Technical jargon refers to specialized language or terms, such as 'security accounts manager' or 'hex format,' that are unlikely to be understood by laypersons. Using such terms in interactive systems can potentially make the user anxious, causing them to question their actions or refrain from using the system further.

concepts.name: User-centric approach
concepts.definition: User-centric approach is a process for designing computer systems by considering the characteristics, needs, and expectations of the users. This method ensures that the system is designed to meet the specific requirements of the people who will use it.

concepts.name: System state
concepts.definition: System state is the exact condition of the system as perceived by the user, focusing on what is happening from the user's point of view rather than technical details. This perception helps the user understand the current status of the system.

concepts.name: Goal state
concepts.definition: Goal state is the final condition a user reaches after transitioning through various states to successfully complete a desired task or work. Users transition between states until they achieve this ultimate goal.

concepts.name: Layouts
concepts.definition: Layouts are the methods by which interface elements are organized on a screen or interface. These arrangements must meet the expectations of the user.

concepts.name: User characteristics
concepts.definition: User characteristics refers to the specific traits and knowledge of the user that must be understood during system design. Knowledge of these characteristics is essential for building an appropriate system.

concepts.name: Interface
concepts.definition: Interface is the mechanism provided to the user that allows them to input information, view outcomes, and act based on those outcomes. The required interface depends heavily on the user's technical expertise.

concepts.name: Querying language
concepts.definition: Querying language is a technical skill or language used by advanced users to retrieve information from a database. This language is typically known by technical experts, unlike general users.

concepts.name: Interactive system
concepts.definition: Interactive system is a system designed for use by laypersons, meaning the users do not need to be technology experts or possess specialized knowledge of technological jargon to understand how the system functions.

concepts.name: Novice
concepts.definition: Novice is the first class of users who are typically using a system for the first time and are unlikely to have prior knowledge of how the system works.

concepts.name: Intermittent
concepts.definition: Intermittent users represent the second class in the three-class user categorization, characterized by occasional usage of the system.

concepts.name: Expert
concepts.definition: Expert is the third class of users who have used a system regularly over a long period of time, allowing them to understand all aspects and use it very efficiently.

concepts.name: User categorization
concepts.definition: User categorization is a method that allows designers to gain a starting point for understanding users by classifying them into distinct groups based on their experience level.

concepts.name: Usability
concepts.definition: Usability is a measure of how good a system is from the point of view of the user. The three primary metrics used to measure usability are effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction.

concepts.name: User-centric design
concepts.definition: User-centered design is the process where users are involved, either actively or passively, in the design lifecycle of a product. This design process aims to create products that increase usability.

concepts.name: User interface designer
concepts.definition: User interface designer is primarily concerned with the creative design of interface elements and layouts, which is informed by the characteristics of the user.

concepts.name: Application software developer
concepts.definition: Application software developer is primarily concerned with the development of software, which is the main focus when building a system.

concepts.name: Development lifecycle
concepts.definition: Development lifecycle is a structured process that must be followed when building software to ensure it accounts for users' characteristics, needs, and expectations, making the system easier to use.

concepts.name: Specified context of use
concepts.definition: Specified context of use is the particular environment or scenario in which a product is designed to be used. Usability is ideally restricted to this specific context rather than all possible usage scenarios.

concepts.name: Effectiveness
concepts.definition: Effectiveness measures whether the user is able to successfully complete the tasks they intend to perform. This metric focuses on goal achievement, distinguishing it from efficiency (speed) and satisfaction (user feeling).

concepts.name: Efficiency
concepts.definition: Efficiency refers to how fast the user can do whatever they want to do.

concepts.name: Extended reality systems
concepts.definition: Extended reality systems are interactive systems designed to create a relationship between the user and the virtual environment. This relationship is fundamentally built through the integration of both software and hardware components.

concepts.name: Interaction design
concepts.definition: Interaction design is the process of modeling how to provide input from the user's point of view, focusing on how easily the user can provide that input. This is a key part of the user-centered design approach.

concepts.name: Perceptual design and modeling
concepts.definition: Perceptual design and modeling is crucial for determining how well the output is generated, ensuring that the generated stimuli are appropriately perceived by the user. This is important because generating and perceiving stimuli are both vital for the system's effectiveness.

concepts.name: XR engine
concepts.definition: XR engine is the middleware component of the system, situated between the hardware and the application layer. This engine utilizes the system's hardware resources to generate output that stimulates the user's senses.

concepts.name: Perceptual design
concepts.definition: Perceptual design is related to ensuring that the output generated for the user is appropriately sensed, understood, or perceived. It is one of the two critical design elements alongside interaction design.

concepts.name: Perceptual system
concepts.definition: Perceptual system is the mechanism that dictates how our senses and perception function, driven by underlying physiology. Understanding this system is necessary to understand how we experience interactive and extended reality systems.

concepts.name: Immersion
concepts.definition: Immersion is the perception that a user is situated within a virtual environment. This feeling is achieved when the system successfully fools the user's perceptual system into believing they are in a familiar, real-world setting.

concepts.name: Perceptual psychology
concepts.definition: Perceptual psychology is the science of understanding how the brain converts sensory stimulation into perceived phenomena.

concepts.name: Sensor
concepts.definition: Sensor is a device that converts an energy source into electrical signals within a circuit. This term is used when discussing a technological system or device.

concepts.name: Human bodily sensor
concepts.definition: Human bodily sensor refers to a body organ that converts a stimulus into neural impulses. Unlike a device sensor, which converts an energy source into electrical signals in a circuit, the human sensor is a biological component of the body.

concepts.name: Mechanoreceptor
concepts.definition: A mechanoreceptor is a receptor that senses motion, vibration, or gravitational force. These receptors are involved in the auditory, touch, and balance senses.

concepts.name: Chemoreceptor
concepts.definition: A chemoreceptor is a receptor that provides signals based on the chemical composition of matter. These receptors are used for the senses of taste and smell.

concepts.name: Vestibular organ
concepts.definition: Vestibular organ is the sense organ that detects gravity or acceleration. It is specifically responsible for the sense of balance.

concepts.name: Photoreceptor
concepts.definition: A photoreceptor is a receptor found in the eyes. It targets electromagnetic energy, specifically in the frequency range of visible light.

concepts.name: Receptor
concepts.definition: A receptor is a sensor that is part of a sensory organ. It is designed to target particular stimuli.

concepts.name: Sensory system selectivity
concepts.definition: Sensory system selectivity is the phenomenon where a receptor is designed to activate only when a specific type of stimulus arrives. For instance, photoreceptors are selective for electromagnetic energy within the frequency range of visible light.

concepts.name: Perception
concepts.definition: Perception is an abstract, higher-level activity that occurs after sense organs convert stimuli into neural impulses. This process is responsible for how we perceive things.

concepts.name: Neuron
concepts.definition: Neuron is a fundamental component of the neural network, possessing a nucleus, dendrites, and an axon. It functions by receiving neural impulses toward the cell body and transmitting impulses away from it.

concepts.name: Synapse
