concepts.definition: Synapse is a gap between the axon of one neuron and the dendrite of the next neuron. Communication occurs across this gap via electrical or chemical signals.

concepts.name: Cerebral cortex
concepts.definition: Cerebral cortex is the part of the brain that handles perception and other functions like attention, memory, and language. Roughly 20 billion neurons are devoted to this task.

concepts.name: Hierarchical processing
concepts.definition: Hierarchical processing is a type of neural processing that occurs in stages, where signals move from initial receptor inputs through successive levels of aggregation until they reach the cerebral cortex. This staged approach allows the detection of increasingly complex patterns within a stimulus.

concepts.name: Selectivity
concepts.definition: Selectivity is the characteristic of a receptor where it responds only to a narrow range of stimuli. This narrow range can be defined across various dimensions, including time, space, or frequency.

concepts.name: Stimuli interpretation
concepts.definition: Stimuli interpretation is the process where the meaning of a stimulus is determined, and it is not based solely on the sensory inputs received. It also depends heavily on the real-life experience and knowledge a person possesses.

concepts.name: Perceptual phenomena
concepts.definition: Perceptual phenomena are the results of combining sensory input with existing knowledge, and they include abilities such as face recognition or identifying a song.

concepts.name: Perceptual processing
concepts.definition: Perceptual processing is the interpretation of stimuli, which results from combining real-time sensory input with long-term knowledge or experience. This process demonstrates that perception is not based solely on raw sensory data but depends heavily on prior knowledge.

concepts.name: Long-term memory
concepts.definition: Long-term memory is where knowledge and life experience are stored, representing information that has been gained or learned over an extended period of time.

concepts.name: Proprioception
concepts.definition: Proprioception is a form of perception that allows the body to sense the relative positions of its parts and the muscular effort used during movement. This sense is unique because it does not rely on a dedicated sensory organ or receptor.

concepts.name: Efference copies
concepts.definition: Efference copies are signals sent by the motor cortex to other parts of the brain. These signals communicate the specific motions that have been executed by the body.

concepts.name: Sixth sense
concepts.definition: Sixth sense refers to a type of perception that functions without a dedicated sensory organ or receptor. This sense is derived from processing information sent by the motor cortex to understand body position and effort.

concepts.name: Sensory conflict
concepts.definition: Sensory conflict is a situation where different sensory inputs, such as vision and proprioception, report contradictory information to the brain.

concepts.name: Human physiology
concepts.definition: Human physiology is a basic concept studied in the context of designing Virtual Reality (VR) systems. It provides foundational knowledge about the body's functions relevant to XR design.

concepts.name: Visual perception
concepts.definition: Visual perception is the process where light arrives on the retina, which is part of the eye, leading to the perception of the scene. This process is guided by both engineered and natural lenses.

concepts.name: Natural lens
concepts.definition: Natural lens is the part of the eyes that is used in the combined lens system. Our eyes naturally contain lenses that contribute to visual perception.

concepts.name: Light propagation
concepts.definition: Light propagation is the movement of light through the combination of lenses. This process eventually leads to the perception of the scene.

concepts.name: Retina
concepts.definition: Retina is a component located at the back side of the eye where the light rays are focused to form images.

concepts.name: Photon
concepts.definition: Photons are tiny particles of energy that move through space at high speeds. This particle view of light is helpful when calculating the amount of light received by a sensor or receptor.

concepts.name: Wave
concepts.definition: A wave is a ripple that travels through space. This description of light as a wave is helpful for understanding the spectrum of color.

concepts.name: Ray
concepts.definition: A ray is a trajectory or path assumed to be created by a single hypothetical photon. This concept of light as a ray is helpful in explaining how lenses work and the concept of visibility.

concepts.name: Transmission
concepts.definition: Transmission is the process where light falls onto a surface, passes through the medium, and subsequently emerges from that surface.

concepts.name: Absorption
concepts.definition: Absorption occurs when a portion of a light ray is absorbed within the material, causing the ray to terminate inside the object. There is no further propagation of the ray outside the material.

concepts.name: Reflection
concepts.definition: Reflection is the phenomenon where a light ray strikes a surface and bounces away without penetrating or entering the object. This process distinguishes it from transmission, where the light passes through the material.

concepts.name: Color perception
concepts.definition: Color perception is the process where a viewer perceives a color based on the intensity of light that reaches their eye. This light is determined by how light rays interact with the surface of an object.

concepts.name: Ambient light
concepts.definition: Ambient light is the light present in the environment that reaches the eye. This light is reflected from the object surface and combines with light coming from a direct source.

concepts.name: Cornea
concepts.definition: Cornea is an outer surface component of the eye that refracts light rays as they pass through it.

concepts.name: Lens
concepts.definition: Lens is a component of the eye that refracts light rays, working in sequence with the cornea to focus images.

concepts.name: Iris
concepts.definition: Iris is the structure that controls the amount of light entering the eye by dilating or constricting the pupil size.

concepts.name: Rods
concepts.definition: Rods are a type of photoreceptor that are more numerous in the peripheral region of the retina.

concepts.name: Cones
concepts.definition: Cones are a type of photoreceptor that are mainly located in a small central region of the retina, which is called the fovea.

concepts.name: Fovea
concepts.definition: Fovea is the central region of the retina that possesses the greatest concentration of photoreceptors, specifically cones. This region is responsible for contributing to the perception of central vision.

concepts.name: Photopic vision
concepts.definition: Photopic vision is the type of vision accomplished only with cones, which allows for the perception of colors and is associated with central vision.

concepts.name: Scotopic vision
concepts.definition: Scotopic vision is the type of vision accomplished only with rods, which is related to peripheral vision and allows weak lights to be visible as a series of grays.

concepts.name: Image acuity
concepts.definition: Image acuity is the ability to perceive fine detail, which is aided by having one optic nerve fiber for each cone.

concepts.name: Visible light
concepts.definition: Visible light is a spectrum of frequencies of electromagnetic light waves. This range encompasses the light waves that fall between the red and violet ends of the spectrum.

concepts.name: Central vision
concepts.definition: Central vision is one of the two types of vision supported by human eyes, which is enabled by the high concentration of cones found in the fovea. This type of vision allows the perception of a sharp color image when the eyes are pointed straight at a target.

concepts.name: Peripheral vision
concepts.definition: Peripheral vision is the other type of vision supported by human eyes, which relies on the peripheral region of the retina. This region has a lower density of photoreceptors and is better at detecting movement than central vision.

concepts.name: Blind spot
concepts.definition: Blind spot is a region in the eye where the individual cannot perceive light or visual stimuli. This area is blind because it lacks photoreceptors.

concepts.name: Image surface
concepts.definition: Image surface is the area of the eye where light rays fall, which is characterized as a non-planar surface. This surface is where the light is received before being transmitted to the brain.

concepts.name: Engineered lens
concepts.definition: Engineered lens is an artificially created lens setup designed to receive parallel lights. These lights converge to a focal point located on the focal plane.

concepts.name: Focal plane
concepts.definition: Focal plane is the specific plane where parallel lights converge when passing through an engineered lens. The distance between the lens and this focal point is known as the focal depth.

concepts.name: Refractive index
concepts.definition: Refractive index is a property of a medium that quantifies the amount of light that passes through it. This index is unique to each medium and affects how light travels through it.

concepts.name: Focal point
concepts.definition: Focal point is the point to which light is converged when entering the eye. This point is the retina center.

concepts.name: Combined power
concepts.definition: Combined power is the total optical strength achieved when multiple lenses, such as the cornea and the natural lens, are used together. This combined power determines whether faraway objects are focused correctly onto the retina.

concepts.name: Diopter
concepts.definition: Diopter is a unit of measurement used to quantify the optical power of a lens. This measurement is necessary to determine if the eye has sufficient power to focus light correctly.

concepts.name: Convex lens
concepts.definition: Convex lens is an optical component that increases optical power, functioning similarly to reading glasses. It is used inside the VR headset to help focus light onto the retina.

concepts.name: Virtual image
concepts.definition: Virtual image is the appearance of the screen as an enormous image that is perceived as being infinitely far away. This differs from a real image, which is physically projected onto the retina and is necessary for the formation of perception.

concepts.name: Focal distance
concepts.definition: Focal distance is the specific distance between the screen and the engineered lens that must be maintained for the best user experience. The engineered lens is usually placed at this distance.

concepts.name: Binocular vision
concepts.definition: Binocular vision is the process of looking at something using both eyes. It involves both eyes seeing the same image within a common region.

concepts.name: Degrees of freedom
concepts.definition: Degrees of freedom is a concept that indicates the different ways an object can move in space. There can be a total of six degrees of freedom in three-dimensional space.

concepts.name: Translational movement
concepts.definition: Translational movement is one of the two primary types of motion in a virtual world, used for navigating within the three-dimensional space. This type of movement is distinct from rotational movement, which is primarily used for changing angles along the translational axis.

concepts.name: Rotational movement
concepts.definition: Rotational movement is a type of movement primarily used for moving at different angles along the translational axis. Broadly, these two types of motions can be found in any virtual world.

concepts.name: Spatial resolution
concepts.definition: Spatial resolution is a consideration that determines how many pixels are needed within a specific square area. This metric is crucial for designing effective displays.

concepts.name: Intensity resolution and range
concepts.definition: Intensity resolution and range define how many intensity values a display can produce, along with the minimum and maximum values. These values must be determined based on how many values can be processed without compromising perceptual quality.

concepts.name: Temporal resolution
concepts.definition: Temporal resolution is a consideration that dictates how fast displays need to change their pixels. This is also referred to as the refreshing or frame rate.

concepts.name: VR displays
concepts.definition: VR displays are engineered systems that should ideally be designed to perfectly match the performance of the visual sense they are trying to fool. This design goal requires understanding the limits of human perception.

concepts.name: Aliasing
concepts.definition: Aliasing is the visual effect where a sharp diagonal line appears jagged or stair-stepped when the image is zoomed out. This effect occurs when the display cannot accurately represent fine details.

concepts.name: Screen door effect
concepts.definition: Screen door effect is an image artifact commonly seen in LCD projectors that makes it appear as if there is a physical screen overlaying the image. This happens due to the way the image is displayed.

concepts.name: Retina display
concepts.definition: Retina display is a type of display that requires a minimum resolution of 326 pixels per linear inch (ppi) to achieve a high level of visual clarity. This concept is suitable for displays viewed from a distance.

concepts.name: Physiology of human vision
concepts.definition: Physiology of human vision refers to the biological makeup of our eyes. This knowledge helps explain how we perceive various elements such as color, depth, and scenes.

concepts.name: Auditory sense
concepts.definition: Auditory sense is the human ability to perceive sound, and the lecture will cover its physiology and relevance to extended reality experiences. This sense is the primary focus of the current lecture.

concepts.name: Sound
concepts.definition: Sound is defined as a wave. This wave is the physical phenomenon that is converted into neural impulses by the ear.

concepts.name: Frequency
concepts.definition: Frequency is a wave property that defines how rapidly a sound wave oscillates, measured as the number of complete cycles per second (Hertz). The range of frequencies audible to a human ear, for instance, spans from 20 to 20,000 Hertz.

concepts.name: Outer ear
concepts.definition: The outer ear is the initial part of the human hearing system that receives sound waves. It contains components like the canal, which amplifies sound pressure for a range of frequencies.

concepts.name: Middle ear
concepts.definition: The middle ear is the section of the hearing system located after the outer ear. It houses the three bones, known as ossicles, which transfer vibrations.

concepts.name: Inner ear
concepts.definition: The inner ear is the final part of the human hearing system, which is roughly the size of a marble. It contains the cochlea, the organ responsible for hearing.

concepts.name: Tympanic membrane
concepts.definition: Tympanic membrane is the membrane that is struck by the wave after passing through the outer ear canal. The membrane's vibration then transfers energy to three bones, which are also known as ossicles.

concepts.name: Cochlea
concepts.definition: The cochlea is the sense organ housed within the inner ear. It converts incoming sound energy, which is a wave, into neural impulses for transmission to the brain.

concepts.name: Auditory perception
concepts.definition: Sound perception is the complex process of interpreting auditory input, moving beyond a simple, single-level understanding of sound. Perception occurs across three distinct levels: social, warning, and primitive.

concepts.name: Social level
concepts.definition: Social level perception is the type of perception that helps individuals carry out social interactions with others.

concepts.name: Warning level
concepts.definition: Warning level perception provides an alert or warning about a specific event or situation.

concepts.name: Primitive level
concepts.definition: Primitive level perception is generally the intuitive understanding of sound, often relating to background noises that individuals tend to ignore.

concepts.name: Psychophysics
concepts.definition: Psychophysics is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena that result from physical stimuli. It is defined as a broader field of study.

concepts.name: Psychoacoustics
concepts.definition: Psychoacoustics is a specific area of psychophysics that focuses on sound. It is the scientific study of perceptual phenomena produced by acoustic stimuli.

concepts.name: Stevens' power law
concepts.definition: Stevens' power law is a well-known result from psychophysics that characterizes the relationship between the magnitude of a physical stimulus and its perceived magnitude. This relationship is mathematically represented as P equals Cm to the power x.

concepts.name: Just noticeable difference
concepts.definition: Just noticeable difference (JND) is a well-known result from psychophysics that refers to the minimum amount a stimulus must change for subjects to perceive the change in at least 50% of trials.

concepts.name: Weber's law
concepts.definition: Weber's law is a principle used to capture the Just Noticeable Difference (JND). This law states that the ratio of the noticeable change in magnitude ($\text{Delta M}$) to the original stimulus magnitude ($M$) is a constant ($C$).

concepts.name: Pitch perception
concepts.definition: Pitch perception is a perceptual phenomenon where the frequency of a sound wave is referred to as pitch. Discrimination ability for pitch decreases as the frequency increases, meaning humans are better at detecting small frequency changes at lower frequencies.

concepts.name: Localization
concepts.definition: Localization is a kind of perception that involves determining the source of a sound. This perception is a key element that must be implemented for the best immersive experience.

concepts.name: Azimuth
concepts.definition: Azimuth is the angle measured in the horizontal plane between the forward direction and the sound source. This angle represents the vector projected onto the horizontal plane.

concepts.name: Elevation
concepts.definition: Elevation is the angle that corresponds to the deviation of the sound source from the horizontal plane. This angle is measured between the actual source direction and the horizontal plane.

concepts.name: Interaural Level Difference
concepts.definition: Interaural Level Difference (ILD) is the difference in sound magnitude as perceived by each ear. This difference can occur when one ear is facing the sound source while the other is in an acoustic shadow.

concepts.name: Interaural Time Difference
concepts.definition: Interaural Time Difference (ITD) is the difference in the arrival time of a sound source to each ear. This difference is caused by the physical distance between the two ears.

concepts.name: Head-related transfer function
concepts.definition: Head-related transfer function (HRTF) models how a person receives sound originating from a specific location in space. This model is relevant for dealing with sound in any system, including Extended Reality (XR) systems.

concepts.name: Binaural sound
concepts.definition: Binaural sound is synthesized using a pair of Head-Related Transfer Functions (HRTF) for both ears. HRTF models how we receive sound from a location in space, depending on the size and shape of the head, ears, and ear canal.

concepts.name: Kinesthesis
concepts.definition: Kinesthesis is the awareness of various parameters associated with movement, such as velocities, acceleration, and forces. Unlike proprioception, which is the awareness of the pose of body parts, kinesthesis describes the dynamics of that movement.

concepts.name: Haptic perception
concepts.definition: Haptic perception is the perception of the overall geometric shape of objects. This shape is inferred through the process of haptic exploration, which involves object handling.

concepts.name: Muscle spindle
concepts.definition: Muscle spindle is a receptor embedded inside each muscle. It reports to the brain about changes in the length of the muscle whenever movement occurs.

concepts.name: Golgi tendon organ
concepts.definition: Golgi tendon organ is a receptor embedded in tendons, which are tough bands connecting muscles to bones. It reports changes in muscle tension associated with muscle movement.

concepts.name: Haptic exploration
concepts.definition: Haptic explorations are methods of perceiving the world through touch. These explorations allow us to perceive the geometric properties of objects around us.

concepts.name: Force feedback
concepts.definition: Force feedback is a method of providing touch sensation stimuli, typically delivered through vibrations from XR applications. Force feedback devices are commonly used in VR systems, such as smart gloves or body suits, to allow users to experience physical forces.

concepts.name: Haptic pin array
concepts.definition: Haptic pin array is a device containing a matrix of pins that is controlled by a computer system. The pins are forced upward as the user's fingertip scans the surface, simulating various textures of an object.

concepts.name: Tangible user interface
concepts.definition: Tangible user interface is a method where real-world objects are used to provide feedback to the somatosensory system. This approach replaces computer-controlled haptic devices by allowing users to interact with physical objects whose virtual avatars exist in the world.

concepts.name: Smell interface
concepts.definition: Smell interface is a device intended to provide chemical stimuli to the nose. It typically utilizes air pumps to spray chemical compounds into the air.

concepts.name: Olfactory display
concepts.definition: Olfactory display is a generic term used to refer to systems that function as smell interfaces. These displays are designed to generate and deliver odor stimuli to the user.

concepts.name: Taste interface
concepts.definition: Taste interface is a device used to simulate the sensation of taste electronically. This simulation often requires placing electrodes over and under the tongue to provide stimulation.

concepts.name: Interactive system
concepts.definition: Interactive system is a type of software system that requires an empirical study stage to ensure it conforms to usability. This requirement differentiates it from other software systems.

concepts.name: Usability
concepts.definition: Usability refers to the quality of a system when considering a specific group of users, a defined context of use, and particular tasks. Usability is not a universal quality that applies to every user, context, or task.

concepts.name: Software development life cycle
concepts.definition: Software development life cycle is a process followed to develop and deploy software. This cycle comprehensively captures and represents the design and development activities required for building the software.

concepts.name: Stages
concepts.definition: Stages are the components that capture or structure the whole development process. Through their connection, they represent how the development process should take place to achieve the desired outcome.

concepts.name: Design space
concepts.definition: Design space is the set of all possible designs for a given problem. The size of this space is determined by the number of elements that must be placed on a screen.

concepts.name: Highly iterative lifecycle
concepts.definition: A highly iterative lifecycle is a software development lifecycle that requires frequent looping between stages. This structure is necessary to account for user feedback and implement a user-centric design approach.

concepts.name: Design prototype evaluate cycle
concepts.definition: The Design prototype evaluate cycle is a specific phase within the development process. This cycle comprises the design stage, prototyping stage, and early evaluation stage.

concepts.name: Requirement gathering stage
concepts.definition: Requirement gathering stage is the initial phase where the project's needs are identified, focusing specifically on gathering requirements from end users in addition to the client. This stage involves methods like contextual inquiry, ethnographic studies, and cultural probes to understand user needs

concepts.name: Design prototype evaluate loop
concepts.definition: Design prototype evaluate loop is an iterative cycle designed to refine early designs based on user feedback. This process involves creating a prototype, evaluating it to identify problems, and modifying the design repeatedly until the evaluation reveals no significantly different problems.

concepts.name: Interface design
concepts.definition: Interface design is one of the two activities within the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, alongside interaction design. This cycle focuses on designing the system from the user's point of view based on user requirements, a process separate from code design.

concepts.name: Code design
concepts.definition: Code design is a separate design part from the design-prototype-evaluate cycle. The cycle focuses on designing the interface and interaction from the user's point of view, while coding and code testing can be performed using traditional software engineering processes.

concepts.name: Empirical study
concepts.definition: Empirical study is a unique stage in interactive system development that involves systematic testing with end users. This stage is required to ensure the product conforms to usability.

concepts.name: Interactive System Development Lifecycle
aliases: Interactive system development life cycles (Agile development idea)
concepts.definition: Interactive System Development Lifecycle is the overall idea or process used to build interactive systems.

concepts.name: Digital preservation
concepts.definition: Digital preservation is the process of using digital media to preserve educational, scientific, and other resources. This method allows for the preservation of information in a digital form.

concepts.name: Satra
concepts.definition: Satra is an authoritative center of Vaishnavite faith in Assam that functions as a living workshop for various visual and performing arts.

concepts.name: Tangible heritage
concepts.definition: Tangible heritage refers to heritage aspects of the island that are physical and can be touched or felt, such as cultural artifacts or architectural structures.

concepts.name: Intangible heritage
concepts.definition: Intangible heritage consists of aspects that cannot be physically touched or felt but are sensed through various means, including traditional skills, knowledge, and performing arts.

concepts.name: Cultural heritage
concepts.definition: Cultural heritage comprises two broad aspects: tangible heritage, which refers to aspects that can be touched and felt, and intangible heritage, which is embedded in the daily and occasional activities of social life.

concepts.name: Ecological heritage
concepts.definition: Ecological heritage refers to the flora and fauna of an island that exists due to its unique geology, geography, and topography. This heritage is a key resource that must be preserved.

concepts.name: Archiving
concepts.definition: Archiving means storing the visual and audio files that capture the heritage information of a particular entity, object, space, or place. This process is a key component of digital preservation.

concepts.name: Digital avatar
concepts.definition: Digital avatar is a digital representation created in the digital space of elements and objects from a physical space. This allows for the preservation of fragile artifacts that might not survive over time.

concepts.name: Heritage preservation
concepts.definition: Heritage preservation is the process of creating an archive of heritage information, which ideally consists of multimedia such as images, videos, audios, and texts. This archive utilizes different sorts of media to document the heritage.

concepts.name: User experience
concepts.definition: User experience refers to the extent of presence felt by users while interacting with the virtual environment, specifically the Majuli Island VR Tour. This concern focuses on how immersed users feel within the virtual island.

concepts.name: Immersive virtual tours
concepts.definition: Immersive virtual tours are a component of the digital heritage preservation system that allows users to experience the heritage virtually. These tours enable users to explore the island in a simulated environment.

concepts.name: Hot spot
concepts.definition: Hot spot is a specific location identified on a map of the island where the tangible and intangible aspects are captured. Capturing these spots allows for the comprehensive capture of the island's entire cultural landscape.

concepts.name: Multimodal archive
concepts.definition: Multimodal archive is a collection created to preserve heritage aspects by combining various data types. This archive includes images, 3D models, videos, and textual descriptions of artifacts.

concepts.name: Usability testing
concepts.definition: Usability testing is a method of evaluation that focuses primarily on how easy a design is to use. This testing is the main focus, rather than solely checking the underlying code.

concepts.name: Requirement gathering
concepts.definition: Requirement gathering is the process of learning about end-user needs and is a key stage in system development. This process aims to gather end-user requirements so that the resulting design ensures usability.

concepts.name: Usability
concepts.definition: Usability is a quality that is measured against a specified context of use. Ensuring usability requires knowing how users behave within that specific work context.

concepts.name: System-centered design
concepts.definition: System-centered design is an approach where the development is driven by the skill and interest of the developer or manager. The main concerns of this design focus on what the developer can easily build using available tools.

concepts.name: End user requirement
concepts.definition: End user requirement specifically refers to the needs of the end user, ensuring the system is usable. These requirements are distinct from technical decisions regarding programming languages or database storage.

concepts.name: Feasibility
concepts.definition: Feasibility refers to requirements related to the practical aspects of development. These requirements include decisions such as developing for a mobile platform or selecting a programming language.

concepts.name: Usability requirements
concepts.definition: Usability requirements are system characteristics, along with many other characteristics, that cannot be expressed in terms of functions. These requirements are typically related to the quality attributes of the software.

concepts.name: Non-functional requirements
concepts.definition: Non-functional requirements are system characteristics that cannot be expressed as functions. These requirements contrast with functional requirements, which refer to system features and abilities to carry out specific tasks.

concepts.name: Functional requirements
concepts.definition: Functional requirements refer to system features and abilities of the system to carry out tasks. These functions are treated as black boxes, generating an output from a provided input.

concepts.name: Interface issues
concepts.definition: Interface issues refers to the design or the qualities of an interface that must be usable. These issues cover how the system interfaces with its environment, users, and other systems.

concepts.name: Contextual inquiry
concepts.definition: Contextual inquiry is an end user requirement gathering method used to collect requirements. This method involves observing users while they perform tasks within their natural work setting.

concepts.name: Natural work setting
concepts.definition: Natural work setting is the specific environment where users perform tasks. This setting serves as the specified context of use for gathering end user requirements.

concepts.name: Semi-structured interview process
concepts.definition: Semi-structured interview process is a method of contextual inquiry that combines two elements. These elements are both interviews and observations of the user.

concepts.name: Usability requirement gathering
concepts.definition: Usability requirement gathering is an essential process for ensuring a usable design, which involves collecting the needs and expectations of users. This process ensures that the final design properly addresses the users' needs.

concepts.name: Contextual inquiry
concepts.definition: Contextual inquiry is a systematic way of carrying out the inquiry process, which is structured into five stages: plan, initiate, execute, close, and reflect.

concepts.name: Passive mode
concepts.definition: Passive mode involves recording or videotaping user activities without an observer present during the activity. The recorded activities are then observed later by the researcher.

concepts.name: Master apprentice model
concepts.definition: The master apprentice model is a principle during inquiry where the observer acts as the apprentice and treats the users as the masters. The purpose of this model is to learn user behavior rather than instructing users.

concepts.name: Plan stage
concepts.definition: The plan stage involves planning the activities of the inquiry, which includes identifying the goals of observation, gathering knowledge about the task domain, and arranging methods for recording observations.

concepts.name: Initiate stage
concepts.definition: The initiate stage requires contacting relevant authorities to obtain necessary permissions and establishing open communication with end users to reduce their anxieties about the observation.

concepts.name: Reflect
concepts.definition: Reflect is the final stage of the inquiry process, which involves analyzing the data that was gathered during the observation period.

concepts.name: Execute stage
concepts.definition: The execute stage is the phase where the actual inquiry takes place, meaning the observation of the users in their work setting occurs.

concepts.name: Execute test stage
concepts.definition: The execute test stage is the phase where observations are actually performed and data is recorded. This stage involves the practical execution of the testing process.

concepts.name: Reflect stage
concepts.definition: The reflect stage is the phase where the observer or experimental team analyzes the data that was collected. This analysis is performed to identify the necessary design goals.

concepts.name: Affinity diagram method
concepts.definition: The affinity diagram method is a technique used to arrange collected data to easily find patterns. This process ultimately leads to the design specification of the design goals.

concepts.name: Idea generation
concepts.definition: Idea generation refers to the final note that is taken by the observer. This process involves generating notes and subsequently refining them using better language.

concepts.name: Groups
concepts.definition: Groups are collections formed by identifying patterns among ideas so that similar ideas with similar patterns can be sorted together into a single unit.

concepts.name: Header
concepts.definition: Header is a pattern that is assigned to a group of ideas. This pattern defines the members of the group and binds the ideas together.

concepts.name: Idea
concepts.definition: Idea is a note taken by an observer that is used when following the affinity diagram. Ideas are the fundamental units that are generated during the observation process.

concepts.name: Display
concepts.definition: Display is the location where generated ideas are gathered after the notes are taken. Display can be a wall, a board, or any other designated area used to hold the collected notes.

concepts.name: Requirement
concepts.definition: Requirement is the identification of what needs to be done to make a product usable. It focuses on what must be achieved rather than how it must be implemented.

concepts.name: Design recommendation
concepts.definition: Design recommendation is a set of suggestions that can be developed based on the analysis of collected data. These recommendations serve as guidelines for the design process.

concepts.name: Guidelines
concepts.definition: Guidelines are design recommendations that can be derived from data collection and analysis. They represent a possible outcome of the reflection stage, but they are not the complete specification of how to implement the system.

concepts.name: Contextual inquiry
concepts.definition: Contextual inquiry is a method available for usability requirement gathering. This process involves specific stages to obtain data, which is then analyzed to produce guidelines or functional specifications for a system.

concepts.name: Software requirements specification (SRS) document
concepts.definition: Software requirements specification (SRS) document is a document for specifying all sorts of requirements, functional as well as non-functional. Generally, the convention followed in SRS is the hierarchical structure of requirements.

concepts.name: Functional requirement specification
concepts.definition: Functional requirement specification is the formal representation of requirements that defines system features in terms of functions. These functions consider the input, output, and overall purpose of the system, often structured using a hierarchical convention.

concepts.name: Hierarchical structure of requirements
concepts.definition: Hierarchical structure of requirements is a convention used in specification where requirements are organized in levels, such as R1, R1.1, and so on, to represent functions.

concepts.name: Design guideline
concepts.definition: Design guideline is an output derived from the group-wise organization of notes taken during contextual inquiry, utilized to ensure usability in subsequent design stages. Guidelines are one possible utilization of identified usability requirements, alongside functional requirements which are directly implementable as code.

concepts.name: Function
concepts.definition: Function is a way to frame a requirement derived from contextual inquiry findings. It accepts a specific input, such as a date, and generates a specific output, such as a timetable or list of deadlines, making it amenable to specification and direct conversion into code.

concepts.name: Know the user
concepts.definition: Know the user is the first stage of the requirement gathering process. This stage involves identifying and understanding the different groups of people who will use the system.

concepts.name: Subset of data
concepts.definition: A subset of data is a limited portion of a larger data set that is made accessible to a specific user group. This approach reduces the overall expanse of information, which helps prevent user confusion and cyber sickness.

concepts.name: Usable system
concepts.definition: Usable system is a system designed to meet the needs and expectations of specific, identified user groups. Usability is strictly targeted only for these defined groups and not for all possible users or contexts.

concepts.name: Location awareness
concepts.definition: Location awareness is the ability to ensure users have accurate location information within a virtual environment. Location awareness prevents disorientation, which is especially crucial when users are exploring large geographical spaces.

concepts.name: Tangible and intangible heritage experience
concepts.definition: Tangible and intangible heritage experience is the requirement to provide users with both tangible and intangible heritage. The key challenge is determining how to combine these two elements to create a seamless and cohesive experience for the user.

concepts.name: Interaction aid
concepts.definition: Interaction aid is support provided to improve the overall user experience in a virtual environment. This support includes navigation assistance, user-friendly interfaces, and methods to increase presence through natural interactions.

concepts.name: Contextual inquiry phase
concepts.definition: Contextual inquiry phase is a stage of research used to identify specific issues faced by users. This phase helps pinpoint problems, such as location awareness issues, tailored to specific user groups.

concepts.name: Interface and interaction design
concepts.definition: Interface and interaction design is the design stage of the design-prototype-evaluate cycle, focusing on the basic concepts of how to start the design process and how to represent the resulting design using a design language.

concepts.name: Design language
concepts.definition: Design language is the necessary framework used to express a design, allowing designers to brainstorm or refine the concepts they are developing.

concepts.name: Heuristics
concepts.definition: Heuristics are guidelines, thumb rules, or checklists that can be used as a starting point to aid the creative thinking process in design.

concepts.name: Specification of design
concepts.definition: Specification of design refers to the language used to express design ideas, which is distinct from the specification of requirements. Specification of design can utilize different languages, such as those used to specify interface design versus those used to specify code design.

concepts.name: Prototype
concepts.definition: Prototype is a lightweight implementation used to test a design idea in practice. Prototypes require significantly fewer resources, skilled manpower, and cost compared to a full implementation.

concepts.name: Specific guideline
concepts.definition: Specific guideline is a guideline that is applicable to particular systems or aspects, such as those designed to minimize cyber sickness in VR systems. These guidelines are typically relevant when immersion is a very important issue.

concepts.name: Generic guideline
concepts.definition: Generic guideline is a guideline that is applicable to any interactive system, including extended reality systems. These guidelines may not be fully applicable, but they are mostly applicable to extended reality systems.

concepts.name: Internal consistency
concepts.definition: Internal consistency means that the same elements and interactions should be utilized in other parts of the design when performing the same task. Separate objects or interactions should not be used for the same task in different usage instances.

concepts.name: External consistency
concepts.definition: External consistency ensures that the knowledge a user brings from the real world is as closely matching with their experience in the virtual world as possible. The elements and interactions performed should be close to real-world experience.

concepts.name: Universal usability
concepts.definition: Universal usability is a design principle that requires systems to have facilities for all classes of users, including novices, intermittent, and experts. This approach aims to design systems that support different user categories rather than specific categories.

concepts.name: Informative feedback
concepts.definition: Informative feedback is the provision of information to the user regarding the system's status or the outcome of their actions. This feedback helps the user understand what the system is doing and how much of a task has been completed.

concepts.name: Closure
concepts.definition: Closure is the feeling the user receives when they successfully complete an objective or task within the system. The system must be designed to indicate that the task has been started, executed, and finally completed.

concepts.name: Activity grouping
concepts.definition: Activity grouping is the design principle of organizing a task into distinct parts: a beginning, a middle, and an end. This structure helps the user understand the process and how to proceed toward achieving their goal.

concepts.name: Error prevention
concepts.definition: Error prevention is a design strategy that aims to minimize the possibility of users making mistakes in the first place. This is achieved by designing the system to keep error rates low.

concepts.name: Reversal of action
concepts.definition: Reversal of action is a design objective that allows users to undo or rectify mistakes by returning from an erroneous situation. This is often facilitated by facilities such as undo and redo.

concepts.name: User control
concepts.definition: User control is the design principle that ensures users feel they are in charge of the system. This feeling is crucial because users, especially lay persons, may lack technical expertise.

concepts.name: Feedback
concepts.definition: Feedback is the ability for the user to perceive that an interaction is occurring and that a change in the system state has taken place. It ensures that the user remains in control by making the results of their actions understandable.

concepts.name: Short term memory
concepts.definition: Short term memory is a form of non-permanent storage that functions like a notebook, holding information brought from long-term memory to assist with daily activities.

concepts.name: Long term memory
concepts.definition: Long term memory is the permanent storage that holds information which is retrieved and brought into short-term memory to support current activities.

concepts.name: Short term memory load
concepts.definition: Short term memory load refers to the total amount of information that a user must actively hold in their short-term memory while operating an interface.

concepts.name: Object interaction
concepts.definition: Object interaction is the selection and manipulation of objects that are part of the virtual environment. This process allows users to engage with elements within the virtual space.

concepts.name: Navigation
concepts.definition: Navigation refers to the act of moving from one specific point to another within the virtual environment. This allows the user to traverse the virtual space.

concepts.name: Interaction for system control
concepts.definition: Interaction for system control involves interactions required to change system-related settings. These interactions manage the overall parameters of the environment, distinguishing them from object manipulation or navigation within the virtual space.

concepts.name: Navigation
concepts.definition: Navigation is the act of moving from one point to another within the virtual world, which requires a corresponding change in the user's viewpoint. This technique primarily involves movement rather than object engagement.

concepts.name: Interaction for selection
concepts.definition: Interaction for selection is the process of choosing a specific object from a set of objects within a virtual world. This action identifies the object that the user intends to interact with next.

concepts.name: Interaction for manipulation
concepts.definition: Interaction for manipulation is the second type of object interaction, occurring after an object has been selected. Manipulation of the object involves interacting with it to change the object's properties.

concepts.name: Object selection techniques
concepts.definition: Object selection techniques are methods used to specify one or more virtual objects from a set within a virtual experience. The suitability of these techniques is determined by a set of parameters that influence user performance during the selection task, such as object distance, size, and surrounding density.

concepts.name: Target occlusion
concepts.definition: Target occlusion occurs when a target object is partially or fully hidden by other surrounding objects in the virtual environment. This condition makes locating and selecting the target a challenging task for the user.

concepts.name: Pointing-based selection
concepts.definition: Pointing-based selection is a technique where the user extends a ray into the virtual world to indicate which object they wish to select. This method allows the user to select an object by having the ray intersect it.

concepts.name: Image plane selection
concepts.definition: Image plane selection is a method of selection where the user uses fingers or hands to pinpoint an object on a 2D view plane. This technique defines the object within the plane as viewed by the user from a distance.

concepts.name: Hand selection technique
concepts.definition: Hand selection technique is the method of selecting virtual objects within the virtual world using the user's hand. This category encompasses various techniques that utilize the hand for object interaction.

concepts.name: Virtual hand
concepts.definition: Virtual hand is an avatar of the physical hand that is visible in the virtual world. This virtual hand is tied to the user's physical hand, allowing for a direct one-to-one mapping of motion.

concepts.name: Go-go technique
concepts.definition: Go-go technique is a method designed to select distant objects without causing user fatigue. This technique allows the user to interactively change the length of the virtual arm.

concepts.name: Prism
concepts.definition: Prism is an improvement upon the go-go technique that controls movement based on speed. This technique applies scaled-down motion to the virtual hand when the user's hand movement is slower than a specified minimum velocity.

concepts.name: Intent-driven selection
concepts.definition: Intent-driven selection is a method where the user indicates their desire to select an object using gestures or the posture of their virtual fingers. This technique allows the user to signal their confidence in selecting an object.

concepts.name: Ray casting
concepts.definition: Ray casting is a basic technique where the user points at objects using a virtual ray, which can be either a short line segment or an infinite line. This virtual ray is attached to the user's hand, head, or eye depending on the input device used.

concepts.name: Bend cast
concepts.definition: Bend cast is an improvement over basic ray casting where the system bends the ray toward the object that is closest to the ray's path. This technique reduces the need for precise pointing by identifying the closest object.

concepts.name: Depth ray
concepts.definition: Depth ray is a technique used to resolve ambiguity when a pointing vector intersects multiple targets. It selects the object that is closest to a specific depth marker used for disambiguation.

concepts.name: Eye gaze pointing
concepts.definition: Eye gaze pointing is a method of pointing where the ray is extended and controlled by tracking the user's eye gaze using eye trackers. Changes in the user's eye gaze directly change the pointing direction.

concepts.name: Volumetric selection
concepts.definition: Volumetric selection enables the user to select a three-dimensional region within virtual space. Corresponding objects located within that defined 3D region are then selected.

concepts.name: Head crusher technique
concepts.definition: Head crusher technique involves the user positioning the thumb and forefinger around a desired object. The object is enclosed by the thumb and forefinger within the 2D image plane.

concepts.name: Cone casting flashlight technique
concepts.definition: Cone casting flashlight technique extends the ray casting idea by using a cone instead of a ray. A cone is cast to a distance, and all objects found within the cone's extent are selected.

concepts.name: Two-handed box selection technique
concepts.definition: Two-handed box selection technique allows the user to use both hands to define, orient, and shape a selection volume. This volume can be a cube, a box, or a rectangular parallelepiped.

concepts.name: Manipulation
concepts.definition: Manipulation is the process of modifying the properties of a selected object, such as its position, orientation, scale, shape, color, texture, or behavior. These properties are what are changed when using manipulation techniques.

concepts.name: Hand manipulation
concepts.definition: Hand manipulation utilizes a virtual hand to directly modify virtual objects, often implemented through hand selection, smart gloves, or gesture-based interaction. This technique is distinct from indirect manipulation, which involves using intermediary objects to affect the desired virtual object.

concepts.name: Indirect manipulation
concepts.definition: Indirect manipulation allows a user to modify a desired virtual object by interacting with a separate object that is mapped to it. This enables users to manipulate virtual objects without directly interacting with the virtual object itself.

concepts.name: World in miniature
concepts.definition: World in miniature is an indirect proxy technique that provides the user with a miniature handheld model of the virtual environment. The user can then indirectly manipulate the actual virtual object by interacting with its representation in this miniature model.

concepts.name: Integrated hybrid manipulation
concepts.definition: Integrated hybrid manipulation is a technique where the system automatically switches between selection and manipulation modes without explicit user input. It also switches back to selection mode after the manipulation task is finished.

concepts.name: Navigation
concepts.definition: Navigation is the process of moving the user from one point to another within the virtual world. This movement is characterized by a change in the user's field of view or viewpoint.

concepts.name: Exploration
concepts.definition: Exploration is a type of travel that occurs when there is no explicit goal for the user to reach. The user simply moves around to observe, learn, or explore the environment.

concepts.name: Search
concepts.definition: Search is a type of travel that involves moving toward or looking for a specified target location. This contrasts with exploration, as the user has a specific destination in mind.

concepts.name: Maneuvering
concepts.definition: Maneuvering refers to short, precise movements that change the point of view or viewpoint. This technique involves breaking down a larger path into smaller, focused segments.

concepts.name: Wayfinding
concepts.definition: Wayfinding is the necessary support required for a system to provide a good immersive user experience. Wayfinding support ensures that travel supports are effectively used and deployed by the user while they are navigating.

concepts.name: Walking-based locomotion
concepts.definition: Walking-based locomotion is a technique for traveling in a virtual world by physically walking in the real world. It involves some form of physical movement that corresponds to virtual movement in the immersive environment.

concepts.name: Partial gait technique
concepts.definition: Partial gait technique refers to a scenario where the user walks but remains in the same physical location. The pattern of walking in that single place is mapped to different types of walking in the virtual space.

concepts.name: Gait negation technique
concepts.definition: Gait negation technique requires a specialized setup where the user's lateral movements are canceled, keeping their physical position fixed. The system then maps the remaining movement pattern to a specific type of virtual movement.

concepts.name: Steering-based navigation
concepts.definition: Steering-based navigation is a method that indicates continuous control of direction and speed while the user is moving from one point to another. Essentially, if a system implements continuous control over direction and speed, it utilizes this type of navigation.

concepts.name: Spatial steering-based navigation
concepts.definition: Spatial steering-based navigation is a continuous locomotion technique where the user controls direction and speed using their body parts. This includes methods like gaze-directed movement, allowing travel to follow where the user is looking.

concepts.name: Selection-based navigation or locomotion technique
concepts.definition: Selection-based navigation or locomotion technique allows users to focus on the destination rather than specifying how to reach it. Unlike previous techniques, the user selects where to go instead of continuously specifying the movement path.

concepts.name: Target selection-based locomotion
concepts.definition: Target selection-based locomotion occurs when the user selects a specific destination or target location. Upon selection, the virtual viewpoint changes, allowing the user to feel as if they have moved to the target.

concepts.name: Manipulation-based locomotion techniques
concepts.definition: Manipulation-based locomotion techniques work by manipulating the user's position, orientation, or scale. This manipulation is achieved using gestures that control either the virtual viewpoint or the virtual world.

concepts.name: Mental model
concepts.definition: Mental model refers to the cognitive map of the surroundings and overall environment that a user builds. This model allows the user to easily locate themselves and identify a suitable path to their destination.

concepts.name: Landmark knowledge
concepts.definition: Landmark knowledge is a type of spatial knowledge that refers to having knowledge about specific landmarks within the surroundings or in other locations. This knowledge is essential for constituting the overall mental model.

concepts.name: Procedural knowledge
concepts.definition: Procedural knowledge is a type of spatial knowledge that refers to the sequence of actions required to successfully follow a path. This knowledge is necessary for building the complete mental model of the environment.

concepts.name: Topological knowledge
concepts.definition: Topological knowledge is a type of spatial knowledge that refers to the overall map of the environment. This knowledge, along with landmark and procedural knowledge, forms the essential knowledge base for the mental model.

concepts.name: Landmark
concepts.definition: Landmark is any obvious, distinct, non-mobile object that is positioned within a given place. A good landmark must be clearly visible from different points of view and locations.

concepts.name: Path following
concepts.definition: Path following is a wayfinding support technique where multiple paths through a single space are denoted, often using colors. This allows the user to understand that various routes are available to reach a destination.

concepts.name: Breadcrumbs
concepts.definition: Breadcrumbs is a support idea that involves leaving a trail of markers along a path followed by predecessors. This trail allows users to know which paths have been explored, preventing them from getting lost.

concepts.name: Multimodal interaction techniques
concepts.definition: Multimodal interaction techniques are methods that combine multiple interaction techniques simultaneously for system control. For example, a user can combine voice commands with gestures to perform a task.

concepts.name: Interface and interaction
concepts.definition: Interface and interaction refers to the specific design focus area that was discussed, dealing with how the user interacts with the system. This focus was maintained because the design approaches for code and system design were considered standard.

concepts.name: Interaction techniques
concepts.definition: Interaction techniques are various methods typically used in immersive settings. These techniques include object interaction, navigation interaction, and interactions for system control.

concepts.name: User experience design
concepts.definition: User experience design is the process of designing an experience by first identifying the user. This identification is the first stage in the overall experience design process.

concepts.name: Boat ride experience
concepts.definition: A boat ride experience is a design element intended to give the user the feeling of being transported from one bank of a river to another. This feeling is implemented at the very start of the tour.

concepts.name: 360-degree boat ride video
concepts.definition: A 360-degree boat ride video is a specific type of video used to make the user feel as if they are actually traveling through a boat. This video facilitates the feeling of transport from the mainland to the island.

concepts.name: Pre-processing
concepts.definition: Pre-processing is the initial content processing performed on collected images and videos to improve the visual appearance and quality of the user experience.

concepts.name: Uniform illumination
concepts.definition: Uniform illumination is the process of editing images to ensure that the lighting effect remains consistent across all captured images, even if they were taken at different times.

concepts.name: 360-degree image
concepts.definition: 360-degree image is a captured image used to model specific places, such as a village or town. These images are arranged to allow users to navigate and gain a sense of direction.

concepts.name: Ambient sound
concepts.definition: Ambient sound refers to natural sounds, such as birds chirping or temple bells, that are integrated into the experience to enhance realism and create an authentic ambience.

concepts.name: Virtual tablet
concepts.definition: Virtual tablet is the main interface that provides users with navigation tools, access to information content, and a video player.

concepts.name: Minimap
concepts.definition: Minimap is a world-in-miniature type of support that provides a sense of orientation for a specific location. It aids navigation by reflecting the arrangement of 360-degree images.

concepts.name: Dual map
concepts.definition: Dual maps are a design technique that utilizes both a global map and a local map. This combination reduces clutter and provides clear navigation support.

concepts.name: Orientation awareness
concepts.definition: Orientation awareness is the ability to provide users with spatial orientation. The mini maps specifically provide dynamic orientation awareness to show users the direction they should move.

concepts.name: Information icon
concepts.definition: Information icon is a visual element that provides further details about a place when it is interacted with by the user, typically in the form of textual information.

concepts.name: View interpolation
concepts.definition: View interpolation is a technique that ensures smooth visual transition by blurring the boundaries between two images. This process allows the user to experience a smooth feeling when moving from one image to another.

concepts.name: Virtual vehicle metaphor
concepts.definition: Virtual vehicle metaphor is a 3D model of a vehicle that facilitates long-distance travel within a tour. This metaphor allows the user to explore an entire island, not just a single space.

concepts.name: Selection-based locomotion technique
concepts.definition: Selection-based locomotion technique is a method where the user selects a destination to initiate travel. This technique utilizes a pre-planned route rather than instantaneous movement or target selection.

concepts.name: Route selection
concepts.definition: Route selection is a selection-based locomotion technique where the route is pre-planned, but the user selects the destination to determine the path. Route selection differs from target selection or instantaneous movement because it involves choosing a route rather than simply jumping to a point.

concepts.name: Video player
concepts.definition: Video player is a component integrated into the tablet interface that allows users to access and view various types of cultural and ecological videos.

concepts.name: Textual description
concepts.definition: Textual description provides additional context about locations and significant spots, thereby enriching the user's understanding and engagement.

concepts.name: Directional arrow
concepts.definition: Directional arrow is a visual element added to the system that guides users toward specific points of interest.

concepts.name: Controlled navigation technique
concepts.definition: Controlled navigation technique is a method implemented to allow users to navigate or teleport using a joystick. This technique reduces abrupt movements that are known to cause discomfort.

concepts.name: Usability evaluation
concepts.definition: Empirical or usability evaluation is the process of evaluating the whole system from the point of view of usability. This evaluation occurs after the code testing is complete.

concepts.name: User requirement gathering
concepts.definition: User requirement gathering is the process of determining what a user needs from a system, which involves utilizing various data collection and analysis techniques. This process was applied to the Majuli Island virtual tour design case study.

concepts.name: Designing the experience
concepts.definition: Designing the experience is the process of creating the overall user experience based on the requirements that were gathered. This stage follows the requirement gathering phase.

concepts.name: System implementation
concepts.definition: System implementation refers to the overall process of realizing design ideas that have been formulated based on requirements. This scope is distinct from code-related implementations, which are not the primary focus of this lecture.

concepts.name: Horizontal prototype
concepts.definition: Horizontal prototype is a representation created using a single sketch. A series of sketches, conversely, allows for a vertical prototype that depicts interaction.

concepts.name: Vertical prototype
concepts.definition: Vertical prototype is a prototype designed to represent interactions and functionalities, rather than just the appearance. Vertical prototypes implement selected features in depth, starting from the first screen through the last action performed.

concepts.name: Low-fidelity prototype
concepts.definition: Low-fidelity prototype is a prototype created without technological intervention, meaning no programming or computer is required. These prototypes are typically constructed using simple materials like paper, cardboard, or wood.

concepts.name: Interface sketch
concepts.definition: Interface sketch is a drawing that depicts major components of an interface and provides a simple illustration to envision the appearance of the interface. Interface sketches allow an idea to be expressed so that others or users can comment on it or provide feedback.

concepts.name: Horizontal prototyping
concepts.definition: Horizontal prototyping is primarily used to represent interface ideas and brainstorm alternative designs, allowing users to provide feedback on the overall concept and usability. This approach focuses on depicting the major components and appearance of the interface but does not detail the sequence of actions or the corresponding changes needed to execute a task.

concepts.name: Storyboarding
concepts.definition: Storyboarding is a series of sketches used to represent interaction. Storyboarding captures the sequence of actions required from the user to complete a specific task.

concepts.name: Keyframe
concepts.definition: Keyframe is a snapshot of the interaction at a particular point in time. Each keyframe shows a specific instance of how the screen appears to the user during the execution of a task.

concepts.name: Low fidelity approach
concepts.definition: Low fidelity approach is a prototyping method that does not rely on computers, allowing for creation using simple media like paper. This method is primarily meant for creating horizontal prototypes.

concepts.name: Medium fidelity approach
concepts.definition: Medium fidelity approach is a prototyping method that uses a computer to create simple prototypes. These prototypes can be utilized to build either horizontal or vertical prototypes.

concepts.name: High fidelity approach
concepts.definition: High fidelity approach is a prototyping method where prototypes are created using computer programs. This process is effectively actual software development, making it more sophisticated and requiring skilled programmers.

concepts.name: Wizard of Oz approach
concepts.definition: Wizard of Oz approach is a prototyping technique where a human subject believes they are interacting with an autonomous computer. In reality, an unseen human operator, known as the wizard, controls the computer and returns the results to the subject.

concepts.name: Throwaway prototypes
concepts.definition: Throwaway prototypes are prototypes used for a quick evaluation and are subsequently discarded. These prototypes are ideally low fidelity, such as paper sketches, because they are inexpensive and fast to create.

concepts.name: Incremental prototypes
concepts.definition: Incremental prototypes involve designing the system into separate units or modules. Each unit is prototyped and tested individually before being integrated into the complete system.

concepts.name: Evolutionary prototypes
concepts.definition: Evolutionary prototypes start with a simpler version of the whole system, which is then tested and refined. Functionalities are progressively added to evolve the prototype into the final product.

concepts.name: Expert evaluation
concepts.definition: Expert evaluation is a technique used for quick and cheap evaluation of prototypes. It is typically performed at an early stage of the design process without requiring significant time or resources.

concepts.name: Evaluation team
concepts.definition: Evaluation team is the group responsible for performing the evaluation of the prototype. This team may consist of the design team itself, skilled designers, or optionally, a few end users.

concepts.name: Usability issues
concepts.definition: Usability issues are a list of problems that are perceived by the evaluator during the testing process. These issues are compiled from individual reports to create a final list.

concepts.name: Cognitive walkthrough
concepts.definition: Cognitive walkthrough is a usability inspection method used to identify usability problems by inspecting a prototype. This technique requires evaluators to perform tasks using the prototype while answering specific questions about the interaction.

concepts.name: Storyboard
concepts.definition: Storyboard is a series of sketches that depicts the changes of the screen after each interaction within a prototype. Essentially, each prototype created for this purpose functions as a storyboard.

concepts.name: Scenario
concepts.definition: Scenario is a task description that evaluators use to perform tasks supported in the prototype. This scenario helps define the specific goal the user is trying to achieve using the interface.

concepts.name: Heuristic evaluation
concepts.definition: Heuristic evaluation is a technique where evaluators check a design prototype against a list of heuristics. Evaluators report findings on whether each heuristic is followed or violated, and provide reasons for any violations.

concepts.name: Recognition rather than recall
concepts.definition: Recognition rather than recall is a principle stating that users should recognize necessary actions from elements rather than being forced to remember information to perform a task.

concepts.name: User evaluation
concepts.definition: User evaluation is a quick feedback technique that requires involving users directly to gather information. This method is often called evaluation with self-reports, where feedback is collected using rating scales.

concepts.name: Expert evaluation technique
concepts.definition: Expert evaluation technique is a method used to quickly evaluate prototypes, such as cognitive walkthrough and heuristic evaluation. These techniques are distinct from user evaluation because the involvement of users is optional.

concepts.name: Likert scale
concepts.definition: Likert scale is a rating scale used to record participant responses, such as those gathered on the previous presence questionnaire (QEP). It utilizes a defined numerical range, such as 1 to 7, to quantify these responses.

concepts.name: System Usability Scale
concepts.definition: System Usability Scale (SUS) is a popular post-session questionnaire designed to measure the overall usability of a system. This questionnaire consists of 10 statements, which are rated on a 5-point agreement scale.

concepts.name: Virtual reality sickness questionnaire
concepts.definition: Virtual reality sickness questionnaire (VRSQ) is a relevant questionnaire used for evaluating experiences within virtual reality. It is particularly useful when assessing VR experiences utilizing Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs).

concepts.name: Empirical evaluation
concepts.definition: Empirical evaluation is a stage in system development that ascertains whether the developed system is usable by assessing it with end users. This stage is crucial for determining the usability of the system after the code testing stage.

concepts.name: Empirical study
concepts.definition: Empirical study is a type of research that involves observation in the real world using real users. This evaluation is conducted after the system is fully implemented to gain an idea of the overall usability of the system.

concepts.name: Fully implemented system
concepts.definition: Fully implemented system is a complete version of the system that is required for conclusive usability evaluation. This type of evaluation cannot be performed on prototypes.

concepts.name: Controlled experiment
concepts.definition: Controlled experiment is a standard method for carrying out research that requires carefully defining participants, managing the setup (including hardware, software, and questionnaires), and defining a procedure designed to eliminate possibilities of biases.

concepts.name: Usability study
concepts.definition: Usability study is a specific type of controlled experiment used in this context to evaluate how well a system functions for a user. This process allows researchers to assess the overall usability aspects of a system.

concepts.name: Identification of research questions
concepts.definition: Identification of research questions is the first stage of empirical research, requiring the formulation of questions for which answers are sought. This process must be completed before the determination of variables can begin.

concepts.name: Determination of variables
concepts.definition: Determination of variables is the second stage of the process, requiring the identification of different types of variables after the research questions have been formulated. Identifying these variables is necessary to successfully design and execute a controlled experiment.

concepts.name: Design of experiment
concepts.definition: Design of experiment is the crucial third stage, involving both the design of the experiment and the subsequent collection of data through the execution of that design. This stage is considered the core of the process where data collection is planned.

concepts.name: Analysis of the data
concepts.definition: Analysis of the data is the final, rigorous stage of the empirical research process. This involves properly, scientifically, and objectively analyzing the collected data so that the resulting conclusion about the system's usability is reliable.

concepts.name: Research question
concepts.definition: Research question is the fundamental query that guides an empirical study. It is framed to determine the specific knowledge or answer that the experiment aims to find.

concepts.name: Testable question
concepts.definition: Testable question is a research question that allows for the collection of objective data through a controlled study. Testable questions enable the drawing of definitive conclusions based on objective information, unlike non-testable questions which rely purely on subjective user interpretation.

concepts.name: Untestable question
concepts.definition: Untestable question is a research question that cannot be objectively tested through a controlled experiment. These questions rely purely on subjective interpretation and feedback.

concepts.name: Objective data
concepts.definition: Objective data refers to measurable information, such as text entry speed, collected through controlled experiments. This data is gathered irrespective of a user's subjective interpretation or personal feedback.

concepts.name: Independent variable
concepts.definition: Independent variable is a variable that is controlled by the researcher during an experiment. These variables are manipulated to observe their effect on other variables.

concepts.name: Factor
concepts.definition: Factor is a term used interchangeably with independent variable. It represents the variable that is controlled and manipulated during an experiment.

concepts.name: Level
concepts.definition: Level is a specific value assigned to a factor or independent variable. Factors combined with their levels define the distinct test conditions used to design the experiment.

concepts.name: Dependent variable
concepts.definition: Dependent variable is a variable whose value depends on the independent variable or its levels. It is the variable that is measured to see if it changes based on the manipulation.

concepts.name: Test condition
concepts.definition: Test condition is created by combining the factors with their assigned levels. These conditions define the specific setup required for running the experiment.

concepts.name: Empirical
concepts.definition: Empirical means observation in the real world of real users.

concepts.name: Research question framing
concepts.definition: Research question framing is the process of converting broad, generalizable questions that are untestable into multiple testable research questions. These testable questions allow for the collection of objective data, which can then be combined to draw conclusions about the original untestable goals

concepts.name: User profile
concepts.definition: User profile is a detailed description of a user based on well-defined characteristics, such as age, educational background, socio-economic status, and cultural background. This profile is essential for carefully selecting a representative subset of participants to ensure the validity and reliability of experimental conclusions.

concepts.name: Homogeneous user group
concepts.definition: A homogeneous user group is a collection of users that generally share similarities in their backgrounds. These similarities can include educational, socio-economic, or cultural backgrounds.

concepts.name: Number of participants
concepts.definition: Number of participants refers to the quantity of users engaged in an empirical study, which must be sufficient to draw reliable conclusions. Generally, using between 12 and 25 participants is considered adequate for reliable data collection.

concepts.name: Representative task
concepts.definition: Representative task is a carefully chosen task or set of tasks that reflects the activities most frequently used by the potential user group when the interface is deployed in practice. For specific tasks, such as typing, representative tasks are selected based on certain metrics and measures rather than being a random piece of text.

concepts.name: Task performance data
