concepts.definition: Task performance data is the information collected when participants carry out tasks during an experiment. This data is intended to be mostly objective and is analyzed to reach a conclusion about the interface.

concepts.name: Within-subject design
concepts.definition: Within-subject design is a study design where every participant performs tasks corresponding to all test conditions. This means all participants are given every task in the experiment.

concepts.name: Between-subjects design
concepts.definition: Between-subjects design is a study where tasks are distributed among different participants. In this design, not every participant performs all the tasks corresponding to all test conditions.

concepts.name: Practice effect
concepts.definition: The practice effect is a phenomenon where a user's performance improves simply because they have practiced the tasks. This improvement is due to the inherent human nature of acquiring skills while practicing.

concepts.name: Latin square design
concepts.definition: A Latin square design is a systematic method of varying the sequence of tasks assigned to each participant. This variation is used to nullify the effect of the practice effect.

concepts.name: Data analysis
concepts.definition: Data analysis is the final stage of system implementation, addressing the question of what to do with the empirical data collected during the experiment. Data analysis allows us to use the collected data for drawing conclusions on the efficacy of our design.

concepts.name: Statistical significance
concepts.definition: Statistical significance is the determination of whether a difference between means was obtained by chance or due to the test conditions. If a difference is statistically significant, it means the result is reliable and not random.

concepts.name: Mean or average
concepts.definition: Mean or average is a starting statistic used in data processing, representing the average of a group of data items within a sample.

concepts.name: Parametric tests
concepts.definition: Parametric tests constitute one group of statistical significance tests, contrasted with the other group known as non-parametric tests. Examples of parametric tests covered include the paired sample t-test, one-way ANOVA, and repeated measures ANOVA.

concepts.name: Paired sample T test
concepts.definition: Paired sample T test is a specific statistical test used for within-subject designs to compare the means of two related groups. This test helps determine if the difference between the two means is statistically significant.

concepts.name: Quick evaluation
concepts.definition: Quick evaluation is a stage of the design prototype evaluation cycle that is performed after the prototype is implemented. This evaluation does not require the full system to be ready.

concepts.name: Empirical study
concepts.definition: Empirical study is the process of collecting data from end users by means of a controlled experiment, often utilizing questionnaires for data collection.

concepts.name: QEP questionnaire
concepts.definition: QEP questionnaire is a revised version of the presence questionnaire proposed in 2004. It is used specifically for the measure of presence.

concepts.name: Presence questionnaire
concepts.definition: Presence questionnaire is a standard questionnaire designed to measure the psychological state of presence. A revised version of this questionnaire was proposed in 2004.

concepts.name: Familiarity bias
concepts.definition: Familiarity bias is a potential issue where participants who are already familiar with VR systems produce results different from those who are not. This bias can lead to incorrect conclusions based on the analysis of the obtained data.

concepts.name: Pre-exposure assessment
concepts.definition: Pre-exposure assessment is a measurement conducted before the user is exposed to the system. This assessment serves to establish a baseline data point for comparison after the user has interacted with the system.

concepts.name: SSQ Questionnaire (Sickness Questionnaire)
concepts.definition: SSQ Questionnaire (Sickness Questionnaire) is the specific instrument used to collect data and measure the severity of cyber sickness in both pre and post exposure situations.

concepts.name: Wilcoxon signed rank test
concepts.definition: Wilcoxon signed rank test is a statistical significance test performed to determine if the observed differences between pre and post exposure scores are statistically significant.

concepts.name: Requirement gathering
concepts.definition: Requirement gathering involves collecting functional and non-functional requirements, which include usability requirements. Various methods, such as contextual inquiry, are used during this stage to gather input from both end users and clients.

concepts.name: Empirical study
concepts.definition: Empirical study is a method used to estimate usability by identifying participants and gathering their time. This study helps determine if there are still gaps in the system's usability.

concepts.name: Design document
concepts.definition: Design document is a document required during the design phase. It encompasses documentation for interface design, interaction design, and code design.

concepts.name: Agile development framework
concepts.definition: Agile development framework is a development approach that prioritizes quick turnaround and continuous feature delivery, working in small, iterative cycles rather than completing the entire system before delivery, as is done in standard methods.

concepts.name: Iteration
concepts.definition: Iteration, also known as a sprint, is the development cycle that includes requirements, development, testing, and delivery. This cycle is typically short, lasting four to six weeks.

concepts.name: Inception
concepts.definition: Inception is an initial stage that involves the creation of the team and the arrangement of necessary funds and resources. This stage, along with conceptualization, refers to requirement gathering.

concepts.name: Release
concepts.definition: Release is a stage in the process flow that includes testing, training, and documentation. This stage follows the development cycle and precedes production.

concepts.name: Agile development method
concepts.definition: Agile development method is a practical way of building interactive systems when compared to standard system development life cycles.

concepts.name: Optimization
concepts.definition: Optimization is a strategy used to reduce the size of an application and decrease associated computations, including memory access.

concepts.name: Optimized experience (psychophysiological experience optimization)
concepts.definition: Optimized experience (psychophysiological experience optimization) is one of the two perspectives used to view optimization in VR. This perspective focuses on the user's psychophysiological experience.

concepts.name: Optimized resource utilization (technological optimization)
concepts.definition: Optimized resource utilization (technological optimization) is the second perspective for discussing optimization in VR. This perspective relates to the resource requirement of the system.

concepts.name: Experience optimization
concepts.definition: Experience optimization is the process of designing an experience to minimize cyber sickness or the possibility of its induction while using a system. This process is considered an optimization problem.

concepts.name: Resource optimization
concepts.definition: Resource optimization is the effort to build systems that minimize resource requirements in XR or VR. This must be done while ensuring that the immersive experience is not compromised.

concepts.name: Internal factors
concepts.definition: Internal factors are elements related to the user themselves that are primarily responsible for cyber sickness. These factors include the user's age, gender, physical condition, and emotional condition.

concepts.name: External factors
concepts.definition: External factors are elements outside of the user that can induce cyber sickness. These factors are broadly divided into hardware and VR content categories.

concepts.name: Hardware factors
concepts.definition: Hardware factors are external elements related to the physical equipment used in VR that are considered responsible for cyber sickness. These factors include display resolution, latency, and type of input.

concepts.name: Virtual locomotion techniques
concepts.definition: Virtual locomotion techniques are methods used to navigate within a virtual reality world. These techniques allow a user to perform a virtual reality tour in the virtual environment.

concepts.name: User-controlled virtual tours
concepts.definition: System-controlled virtual tours are tours where the application or system dictates the user's travel within the VR environment. The user's movement and navigation are guided by the system itself, often following a predetermined path.

concepts.name: System-controlled tour
concepts.definition: System-controlled tour is a type of tour where the system manages the navigation and movement, providing the user with an effortless experience and reduced cognitive demands. System-controlled tours are the focus of this lecture segment.

concepts.name: Cognitive demand
concepts.definition: Cognitive demand is the mental effort required from the user, which is reduced when the system takes over decision-making tasks such as determining how or which way to move. Reduced cognitive demands allow the user to concentrate more on the experience itself.

concepts.name: Realistic walking experience
concepts.definition: Realistic walking experience is a navigation experience within a system-controlled tour where the user does not feel controlled by the system. This experience is achieved when the difference between realistic and unrealistic elements vanishes in the user's mind, allowing the user to feel present in the tool.

concepts.name: Optic flow
concepts.definition: Optic flow is the speed of change of the scene, which is used to simulate movement in a virtual world. This speed determines how the user perceives movement by observing the surroundings.

concepts.name: VR experience optimization
concepts.definition: VR experience optimization is the process of psychophysiological optimization, specifically framed to minimize cyber sickness prevalence while the user is experiencing the immersive system.

concepts.name: Natural walking experience
concepts.definition: Natural walking experience is the desired outcome of the optimization effort. It involves creating a realistic walking experience within the VR world, particularly in a system-controlled tour.

concepts.name: Realistic walking behavior model
concepts.definition: Realistic walking behavior model is a model of natural walking behavior utilized to address the need for a realistic walking experience in system-controlled VR navigation. Specifically, it helps ensure that the displayed visual speed, or optic flow, matches the user's instantaneous walking speed.

concepts.name: Photograph-clicking task
concepts.definition: Photograph-clicking task is an assigned activity where the user stops at a painting to click a photo, ensuring they stop after walking a predefined distance.

concepts.name: Instantaneous step frequency
concepts.definition: Instantaneous step frequency is the rate of steps taken by the user, which is represented as a function of distance. This frequency is similar or related to the actual speed.

concepts.name: Velocity
concepts.definition: Velocity is the speed of the user, which the study tracked to observe how it changes over time during walking. The user's velocity was observed to increase gradually, reach a maximum, and then decrease before stopping.

concepts.name: Fourier series
concepts.definition: Fourier series is a mathematical series that approximates any continuous periodic function to arbitrary precision by using weighted terms.

concepts.name: Perceived speed
concepts.definition: Perceived speed is the rate of movement that an individual experiences visually, which may not be the same as the actual physical speed of movement.

concepts.name: Visual gain
concepts.definition: Visual gain is a factor multiplied by the actual speed to compute the desired visual speed. This factor is used to obtain a different speed that is perceived as natural.

concepts.name: Actual visual speed
concepts.definition: Actual visual speed is the speed obtained by multiplying the instantaneous speed by the visual gain. This resulting speed is what is perceived as natural.

concepts.name: Actual speed
concepts.definition: Actual speed is the speed at which the user is physically moving, which is related to the instantaneous step frequency. This speed is represented by a specific mathematical formulation.

concepts.name: CISO pattern
concepts.definition: CISO pattern is a specific pattern revealed by studies that is similar to the Fourier transform of sinusoidal waveforms. This pattern allows for the computation of the actual speed.

concepts.name: Instantaneous speed
concepts.definition: Instantaneous speed is the natural walking speed model utilized in the experiment. This speed model is contrasted with a constant speed experience.

concepts.name: Natural walking behavior
concepts.definition: Natural walking behavior is a computed formulation designed to provide the user with a perception of realistic movement within the virtual environment. This model is specifically intended to enhance perceived realism compared to experiences utilizing a constant average speed.

concepts.name: Perceived realism
concepts.definition: Perceived realism is the measure of how real the user experiences the virtual environment to be. The study aimed to confirm whether the usage of the model enhances this perceived realism.

concepts.name: Realistic walking speed model
concepts.definition: Realistic walking speed model is a model designed for system-controlled virtual reality tools. This model maximizes presence by meeting the specific requirements for realism as perceived by the user.

concepts.name: Exposure duration
concepts.definition: Duration of exposure refers to the total time a user spends experiencing a virtual tour. This duration is the primary variable that the optimization process seeks to improve.

concepts.name: Perceived instantaneous walking speed
concepts.definition: Perceived instantaneous walking speed is the walking speed as experienced by the user, which is represented by the visual gain into the actual instantaneous speed. This speed is represented in a specific mathematical form.

concepts.name: Teleportation-type movement
concepts.definition: Teleportation-type movement is a method of navigation where the speed is at its maximum. This results in instantaneous movement occurring between two specific points.

concepts.name: Interaction time
concepts.definition: Interaction time is the specific duration of time required for a user to interact with the virtual objects. This time can be ignored in entirely system-controlled VR tools.

concepts.name: Points of interest
concepts.definition: Points of interest are the nodes in the graph that represent specific locations within the virtual world. These are the locations that the optimized path must cover.

concepts.name: Semi-interactive tour
concepts.definition: A semi-interactive tour is a virtual tour design that imposes a limit on the amount of time a user can spend interacting at any single point of interest. This time limit is used to optimize the overall duration of the experience.

concepts.name: System-controlled VR tool
concepts.definition: A system-controlled VR tool is a virtual reality application where the movement or travel between points is managed automatically by the system. In this scenario, the interaction time can be disregarded.

concepts.name: Optimum path
concepts.definition: Optimum path is the most efficient route designed to meet a specific goal within the virtual tour. This path either ensures all points of interest are visited in minimum time or maximizes the number of points visited within a fixed time.

concepts.name: Weighted graph
concepts.definition: Weighted graph is a representation of the virtual world where the connections between points of interest are assigned numerical values. These weights typically denote the distance between the connected points.

concepts.name: Vertex
concepts.definition: Vertex is a node in the graph that represents a specific point of interest within the virtual world. Each point of interest is assumed to be a vertex in the graph structure.

concepts.name: Edge weight
concepts.definition: Edge weight is the value assigned to an edge between two vertices, representing the Euclidean distance between them if a direct path exists. If the vertices are not directly connected, the edge weight is assigned a very large number, denoted by infinity.

concepts.name: Complete graph
concepts.definition: Complete graph is a graph structure where every vertex is directly connected to every other vertex. This structure is created by adding hypothetical edges to the original graph.

concepts.name: Natural walking speed
concepts.definition: Natural walking speed is the speed used within the natural walking model to compute the travel time between two directly connected nodes. This speed is based on the actual instantaneous walking speed, which is described as realistic.

concepts.name: Actual instantaneous walking speed
concepts.definition: Actual instantaneous walking speed is the realistic speed of the user at any given moment, represented by the variable V act. This speed is derived from the user's step frequency and height.

concepts.name: Total travel time
concepts.definition: Total travel time is the cumulative time required to traverse a distance, which is found by taking an integral of the instantaneous time element over the total distance. This calculation determines the time between two connected nodes.

concepts.name: Travel time estimate tau D
concepts.definition: Travel time estimate tau D is the final computed value for the time between two directly connected vertices. This estimate is derived after applying various mathematical simplifications and Fourier series expansions.

concepts.name: Travelling salesman problem
concepts.definition: Travelling salesman problem is a standard classical problem that is used to find the minimum duration travel within a graph covering all points of interest.

concepts.name: Hamiltonian path
concepts.definition: A Hamiltonian path is a path within a graph that covers all nodes, where each node is visited exactly once.

concepts.name: Hypothetical edge
concepts.definition: A hypothetical edge is an introduced edge used for computation when two vertices lack a direct connection in the original graph.

concepts.name: Modified edge weight
concepts.definition: The modified edge weight is the weight between two nodes, defined as the Euclidean distance if they are directly connected, or the shortest path length if they are not.

concepts.name: Shortest path
concepts.definition: Shortest path is the optimal route between two vertices in the original graph. This path is used to replace any hypothetical edges found in the TSP solver's output.

concepts.name: Travel time
concepts.definition: Travel time is the specific weight assigned to an edge in the modified graph. This weight represents the actual time taken to travel from one vertex to another.

concepts.name: Graph theoretic problem
concepts.definition: Graph theoretic problem is the method of converting the virtual world into a graph structure. This structure uses points of interest as nodes and weighted edges representing the distance between them.

concepts.name: Cybersickness time threshold
concepts.definition: Cybersickness time threshold is a specific time limit in the virtual environment. Crossing this threshold means there is a possibility of cybersickness occurring during the experience.

concepts.name: Time threshold
concepts.definition: Time threshold is the maximum allowed time limit within which a path must be completed. This constraint dictates which paths are viable for the problem statement.

concepts.name: Points of interest
concepts.definition: Point of interest is a given location where the user is expected to spend time to inspect or interact with a particular object.

concepts.name: Importance function
concepts.definition: Importance function is a function (f, v) that assigns a positive real number to every vertex or point of interest. This number indicates the importance of that specific vertex.

concepts.name: Node importance
concepts.definition: Node importance is the measure of how important a specific node is, captured as a positive real number. A higher value of this number signifies a higher importance.

concepts.name: Total importance
concepts.definition: Total importance is the aggregated measure of a given path. This value is calculated by summing the individual importance of every node within that path.

concepts.name: Waiting time
concepts.definition: Waiting time is the time required by a user to inspect or interact with a particular object located at a node. This value represents the maximum time a user needs to spend at that point of interest.

concepts.name: Waiting time function
concepts.definition: The waiting time function is a defined function that maps every node to a real positive number. This number indicates the maximum time required for a user to inspect or interact with the object at that node.

concepts.name: Total waiting time
concepts.definition: Total waiting time is calculated by summing the individual waiting times for all nodes that constitute a specific path. This calculation is performed in a manner similar to calculating total importance.

concepts.name: VRP with profit
concepts.definition: VRP with profit (VRPP) is a generalization of the vehicle routing problem (VRP) where the goal is to maximize profit within given time constraints.

concepts.name: Optimal path P
concepts.definition: Optimal path P is the desired output of the algorithm, representing a route that maximizes the importance (F) of visited nodes while ensuring the total exposure time remains below a specified threshold.

concepts.name: VRPP solver
concepts.definition: VRPP solver is a specialized computational tool used to determine the optimal path by taking the final modified graph, node importance values, and waiting times as input.

concepts.name: Natural walking model
concepts.definition: Natural walking model is a method used to compute the travel time between nodes, ensuring that the resulting travel duration provides a realistic experience.

concepts.name: Cyber sickness issues
concepts.definition: Cyber sickness issues are concerns related to the duration of a virtual experience, as a minimum time path may still be too large to prevent the induction of sickness. Addressing these issues requires finding an optimal path that can be covered within a specific time threshold.

concepts.name: Optimal path approach
concepts.definition: Optimal path approach is a strategy that identifies a path in a virtual world designed to ensure the user explores every point of interest in the shortest possible duration. This approach, however, may still lead to cyber sickness if the virtual world is very large, as the minimum required time to cover all points may be excessive.

concepts.name: Optimal path under time constraint
concepts.definition: Optimal path under time constraint is a method where the user must cover a path that maximizes the number of important points of interest within a predefined time threshold. This constraint sets an upper limit on the duration of the virtual tour.

concepts.name: Points of interest
concepts.definition: Points of interest are specific locations that are identified and used as nodes in the graph formulation for pathfinding. These locations are critical for determining the optimal route.

concepts.name: Graph theoretic form
concepts.definition: Graph theoretic form is the mathematical structure used to model a practical problem so that optimization approaches can be applied to it. This form allows the theoretical concepts to be put into practice.

concepts.name: Graph
concepts.definition: Graph is a structure formulated to represent connections between nodes, where the distance between nodes is measured. This structure allows algorithms to determine optimal paths.

concepts.name: Contextual inquiry
concepts.definition: Contextual inquiry is a field study method used to observe people's travel behavior and gather information about places of importance in their natural environment. This method involves observing users in situ and talking to local people for clarity.

concepts.name: Euclidean distance
concepts.definition: Euclidean distance is a method used to calculate the straight-line distance between two points. This calculated distance is then used as the weight for the edges connecting those points in the graph.

concepts.name: Weight
concepts.definition: Weight is the value assigned to an edge between nodes, typically representing the measured distance between points of interest. While other factors such as relative importance and wait time can be considered for optimization, the simple graph form shown only includes the distance between the nodes.

concepts.name: Resource optimization
concepts.definition: Resource optimization is an objective in extended reality that involves building systems to minimize the requirement of resources. This is done without compromising the user experience, which means maximizing the experience.

concepts.name: Resource requirements
concepts.definition: Resource requirements are the necessary resources that extended reality (XR), particularly virtual reality (VR), needs to operate. Systems must be built to minimize these requirements while simultaneously optimizing the experience.

concepts.name: Resource
concepts.definition: Resource, in a broad sense, can mean hardware, software, manpower, and supporting infrastructure. In the context of VR, this includes specific elements such as input and processing devices, developmental tools, staff, and physical or digital infrastructure like rooms or network gears.

concepts.name: Digital infrastructure
concepts.definition: Digital infrastructure refers to the infrastructure related to the network. This includes network gears, switches, routers, wires, and servers.

concepts.name: Physical infrastructure
concepts.definition: Physical infrastructure refers to the tangible elements supporting a setup. This includes rooms, furniture, and the supply of electricity.

concepts.name: Client end
concepts.definition: Client end refers to the hardware resources that the user has access to. Optimization efforts are focused on the hardware requirements at the client end because it is the most straightforward way to manage resources.

concepts.name: Hardware resources
concepts.definition: Hardware resources are the physical components available to the user that must be optimized to ensure a good experience. These resources are specifically located at the client or user end.

concepts.name: Object
concepts.definition: An object is a geometric shape that can be part of a specific item or part of the overall interface. Objects include the main item and interface elements like menus or icons.

concepts.name: Image
concepts.definition: An image is the entire thing displayed on the screen, which is not limited to just the main object. This whole display is comprised of geometric shapes, and each shape has an attached color.

concepts.name: Synthesis
concepts.definition: Synthesis is the method by which individual represented objects are combined to form a complete, realistic scene. This step transforms isolated parts into a unified, perceivable image.

concepts.name: Generic graphics system
concepts.definition: Generic graphics system is a foundational model used to understand how a static image is rendered, setting it apart from more involved discussions like interactive graphic systems or computer animation. This system includes major components such as a host computer, display, display controller, video memory, and video controller.

concepts.name: Display controller
concepts.definition: Display controller is a major component that receives display commands from the host computer and sends data to video memory for storage. It facilitates two-way communication with the CPU.

concepts.name: Video memory
concepts.definition: Video memory is a major component used for storing data that is sent by the display controller. This stored data is subsequently utilized by the video controller.

concepts.name: Video controller
concepts.definition: Video controller converts the digital image stored in the video memory into analog voltages. Video controller controls the mechanism that activates the pixels on the display screen.

concepts.name: Graphics card
concepts.definition: Graphics card is a dedicated component of a computer designed to handle rendering-related computations. It typically comprises a Graphics processing unit (GPU) and is responsible for processing visual data.

concepts.name: Pixel
concepts.definition: Pixel is a picture element that is arranged in a grid on a graphic display screen. Pixels are activated to emit light, which allows the viewer to perceive a colored image.

concepts.name: Vector scan device
concepts.definition: A vector scan device is a graphic device that renders an image by activating only selective pixels that represent continuous geometric primitives, such as lines or curves. This method assumes that focusing on the rendering of these primitives allows the whole image to be perceived.

concepts.name: Raster scan device
concepts.definition: Raster scan device is a display mechanism that renders images by following a left-to-right, top-to-bottom scanning manner. This sequential scanning causes the excitation of pixels to occur at different times across the screen.

concepts.name: Raster scan displays
concepts.definition: Raster scan displays are the type of display found in commercial products, such as smartphones and televisions, that activate all pixels sequentially across a grid. This rendering arrangement is significantly cheaper compared to the selective rendering required by vector scan devices.

concepts.name: Frame buffer
concepts.definition: The frame buffer is the video memory component of a raster scan system. It contains one memory location corresponding to each pixel, storing the intensity value for that pixel.

concepts.name: Screen refreshing
concepts.definition: Screen refreshing is the periodic re-excitation of pixels to counteract the natural decay of emitted light. This process ensures that the image remains uniform and stable even when the scene itself is not changing.

concepts.name: Refresh rate
concepts.definition: Refresh rate is the number of times a scene is refreshed per second on the screen. It is typically measured in hertz.

concepts.name: Color display
concepts.definition: Color display is a specific type of screen where each pixel contains more than one type of element. These elements are capable of emitting light with different intensities.

concepts.name: Primary color
concepts.definition: Primary color refers to the three fundamental colors—red, green, and blue—that are typically used by elements in a pixel. These colors are emitted with different intensities to represent a combination of colors.

concepts.name: 3D graphics pipeline
concepts.definition: 3D graphics pipeline is a stage-wise process that describes the computation flow. This process starts from the object representation and concludes with the rendering onto the pixel grid.

concepts.name: Graphics pipeline
concepts.definition: Graphics pipeline is the stage-wise process used to compute the values that are stored in the frame buffer. This process ultimately drives the display mechanism via the video controller.

concepts.name: Display processor
concepts.definition: Display processor is the component, which is part of the display controller, that is responsible for computing the necessary values in distinct stages. These values are real numbers stored in the framebuffer.

concepts.name: Object representation
concepts.definition: Object representation is the method used to structure computer-generated scenes, allowing for the depiction of objects that possess varying shapes, sizes, and characteristics.

concepts.name: Modeling transformation
concepts.definition: Modeling transformation is the second stage that moves objects from their individual local coordinate system definitions into a common world coordinate system. This process allows multiple objects of different shapes and sizes to be assembled into a single scene.

concepts.name: Lighting stage
concepts.definition: The lighting stage is the third stage where color is assigned to the constructed 3D scene. Assigning color is crucial because it makes the 3D nature of the scene more prominent and improves visual perception.

concepts.name: Viewing transformation
concepts.definition: Viewing transformation simulates the process of taking a snapshot of a 3D scene through a camera eyepiece. This transformation maps the scene from the 3D world coordinate system onto a 2D device coordinate space, which serves as the equivalent of the screen.

concepts.name: Scan conversion
concepts.definition: Scan conversion is the fifth stage that transforms the continuous device coordinate space description into a discrete pixel grid description. This process maps the real-valued coordinates of the image points to the integer coordinates of the pixels.

concepts.name: Balance
concepts.definition: Balance is the necessary equilibrium between having a representation that captures all intricate details and ensuring that subsequent rendering computations are performed efficiently.

concepts.name: Point sample rendering
concepts.definition: Point sample rendering is a method where information is captured in the form of points on the scene, with each point carrying specific attributes. This process relies on real-world input sensors to generate a synthetic image of the scene.

concepts.name: Boundary representation
concepts.definition: Boundary representation is a technique where objects are defined by the surfaces that delineate the object's boundary. These surfaces can be either polygonal or curved.

concepts.name: Spline representation
concepts.definition: Spline representation is a higher-level method used to represent curved surfaces or curves, typically preferred by designers creating artificial environments. This representation uses several lower-degree polynomials to construct the complete curve.

concepts.name: Viewing pipeline
concepts.definition: Viewing pipeline is the fourth stage of the graphics pipeline, which contains several sub-stages starting with viewing transformation.

concepts.name: Local coordinate system
concepts.definition: Local coordinate system is a definition where an object is represented individually, allowing its position, dimension, and other properties to be defined relative to itself. Essentially, each object is thought of as having its own coordinate reference frame.

concepts.name: World coordinate system
concepts.definition: World coordinate system is a common coordinate system where multiple objects are assembled and defined together to construct a scene. This system allows objects, which are individually defined in their own local systems, to be placed together in a shared setting.

concepts.name: Geometric transformation
concepts.definition: Geometric transformation is the process of applying operations on an object's definition in local coordinates to transform it into the world or scene coordinate system. This stage is necessary to assemble multiple individually defined objects into a cohesive scene.

concepts.name: Basic transformation
concepts.definition: Basic transformation refers to the fundamental operations, such as translation, rotation, scaling, and shearing, that constitute the building blocks of all geometric transformations. Combinations of these basic operations can be used to create any required transformation for scene construction.

concepts.name: Composite transformation matrix
concepts.definition: Composite transformation matrix is a single matrix obtained by combining multiple basic transformations into one. This matrix is used when an object requires several operations, such as scaling and translation, to be moved from its local to the world coordinate system.

concepts.name: Lighting model
concepts.definition: Lighting model is a method used in computer graphics to simulate the process of light reflection and compute the color of a surface point. Lighting models involve a higher degree of computation compared to shading models.

concepts.name: Shading model
concepts.definition: Shading model is an approximation of color assignment that relies on lighting models. Shading models are designed to reduce computational requirements without significantly compromising the quality of the visual experience.

concepts.name: Color computation
concepts.definition: Color computation is the process of assigning colors to objects within a scene. If colors are not assigned properly, the ability to perceive depth in the 3D scene will be negatively affected.

concepts.name: Continuous intensity value
concepts.definition: Continuous intensity value is a real number, typically normalized, that lighting models use to compute colors. These values usually fall within the range of 0 to 1.

concepts.name: Reflection coefficient or reflectivity
concepts.definition: Reflection coefficient or reflectivity is a surface property that determines the fraction of incident light that gets reflected and comes to the viewer's eye. This coefficient varies between 0.0 and 1.0, where 0 represents a dull surface and 1 represents a shiny, mirror-like surface.

concepts.name: Diffuse light component
concepts.definition: Diffuse light component is the intensity of light that comes directly from the source and is reflected in a diffuse manner. This component is one of the three types of light—alongside ambient and specular light—that combine to reach the viewer's eye.

concepts.name: Specular reflection component
concepts.definition: Specular reflection component is the light that is reflected with a specular effect, which appears as a shiny bright spot. This component is calculated using an approximate model, such as the Phong model.

concepts.name: Reflection coefficients
concepts.definition: Reflection coefficients are three-element vectors that specify the reflection properties for the three primary colors: red, green, and blue.

concepts.name: Intensity attenuation over distance
concepts.definition: Intensity attenuation over distance is the phenomenon where the intensity of light diminishes as the distance between the light source and the surface point increases. This factor must be accounted for in realistic rendering.

concepts.name: Radial intensity attenuation
concepts.definition: Radial intensity attenuation is a factor that accounts for the effect of diminishing light intensity based on the distance from the light source. This factor is typically computed using an inverse quadratic function.

concepts.name: Inverse quadratic function
concepts.definition: Inverse quadratic function is a mathematical expression used to compute the attenuation factor for radial attenuation. This function uses the distance between the source and the surface point as a primary variable.

concepts.name: Angular intensity attenuation
concepts.definition: Angular intensity attenuation is a factor used to control light visibility and brightness within a specific region. This factor is primarily considered when generating focused effects like spotlights.

concepts.name: Spotlight effect
concepts.definition: Spotlight effect is a visual outcome where only elements within a defined region are visible or brightly visible. Areas outside this specific zone are rendered darker.

concepts.name: Colored light model
concepts.definition: Colored light model is a method for assigning colors where emitted light intensity is broken down into three components corresponding to the primary colors. These three intensities combine together to give the perception of any color.

concepts.name: Source intensity
concepts.definition: Source intensity is a three-element vector (Is) that represents the light emitted by a colored light source. This vector consists of three components corresponding to the primary colors: red (Isr), green (Isg), and blue (Isb).

concepts.name: Intensity mapping
concepts.definition: Intensity mapping is the process of converting a continuous, infinite range of computed intensity values into a finite set of values supported by a display device. This process involves finding the nearest device-supported intensity value for any computed pixel intensity.

concepts.name: Transformation matrix
concepts.definition: Transformation matrix is a mathematical matrix used to transform a point from its local coordinate system into the world coordinate system. This matrix can be either an individual basic matrix or a composite matrix.

concepts.name: Viewing pipeline
concepts.definition: Viewing pipeline is a set of stages used in computer graphics to simulate the process of rendering a three-dimensional scene onto a two-dimensional display.

concepts.name: Projection
concepts.definition: Projection is the process of selecting a portion of a constructed three-dimensional scene and mapping it onto a two-dimensional display plane or view plane.

concepts.name: Projection transformation
concepts.definition: Projection transformation converts a 3D view coordinate scene to a 2D view plane description, functioning as one of the multiple transformations within the viewing transformation pipeline.

concepts.name: Window-to-viewport transformation
concepts.definition: Window-to-viewport transformation transforms the projected scene from a 2D view plane description to a 2D device coordinate space.

concepts.name: Clipping
concepts.definition: Clipping process is the action of discarding objects that are part of the scene but fall outside of the defined view volume. This process occurs before the projection is performed.

concepts.name: Hidden surface removal
concepts.definition: Hidden surface removal is the process of identifying and eliminating surfaces or objects that are inside the view volume but are not visible to the viewer. This removal is necessary because other objects may occlude them from the viewer's perspective.

concepts.name: View coordinate system
concepts.definition: View coordinate system is a coordinate system that has its own axes (u, n, and v) and is used to represent the scene from the camera's perspective. This system is established based on the parameters of the camera.

concepts.name: Camera parameters
concepts.definition: Camera parameters are the specific values used to define the view coordinate system. These parameters include the camera position, the view of point, the view direction, and the center of interest or look-at point.

concepts.name: Orthogonal axes
concepts.definition: Orthogonal axes are three mutually perpendicular axes (N, V, and U) that are determined using camera parameters. These three axes together define the view coordinate system.

concepts.name: View plane
concepts.definition: View plane is the 2D surface used as the target for projecting 3D objects from the view coordinate system. These planes are typically defined as a rectangular area, which is often called a clipping window.

concepts.name: Clipping window
concepts.definition: Clipping window is a rectangular area that serves as the 2D view plane description onto which 3D objects are projected. This concept is often used interchangeably with the view plane itself.

concepts.name: View volume
concepts.definition: View volume is a three-dimensional region within the scene that determines which portion of the scene will be projected onto the view plane. This volume defines the specific area of the scene that the system is intended to project.

concepts.name: Perspective projection
concepts.definition: Perspective projection is a type of projection that requires converting the frustum into a parallel canonical view volume, which is a normalized unit cube. This conversion involves both scaling and shearing operations.

concepts.name: Parallel projection
concepts.definition: Parallel projection is a type of projection where the canonical view volume can be obtained by simply scaling the arbitrarily defined view volume. This method is computationally simpler than perspective projection.

concepts.name: Canonical view volume
concepts.definition: Canonical view volume is a concept used to simplify pipeline computations in rendering. It involves converting any defined view volume, regardless of its shape or size, into a normalized cube.

concepts.name: Normalized cube
concepts.definition: Normalized cube is a standard cube used to define the view volume. It is the result of converting any arbitrary view volume into a standardized shape and size.

concepts.name: Window
concepts.definition: Window is a normalized clipping window, often referred to as the view plane, which functions as an abstract intermediate representation. Unlike the viewport, the window is not defined in device space or related to the final screen dimensions.

concepts.name: Viewport
concepts.definition: Viewport is a portion of the final screen defined in device space where the scene will be rendered. It is defined with respect to the screen or display origin and dimensions.

concepts.name: VR resource optimization
concepts.definition: Resource optimization in virtual reality is the idea of managing computational issues associated with rendering immersive experiences by taking recourse to different approaches. This is necessary because deploying the whole system for any platform is often not possible.

concepts.name: Projection transformation
concepts.definition: Projection transformation is the process of transforming coordinates from the 3D view coordinate system to the 2D view coordinate system. This transformation is a key step in the graphics pipeline.

concepts.name: Device coordinate system
concepts.definition: Device coordinate system is a continuous coordinate system where the coordinate values can be any real number. This system describes the viewport space before it must be mapped to the discrete integer coordinates of a display's pixel grid.

concepts.name: Pixel grid
concepts.definition: Pixel grid is a structure of a display device that uses discrete coordinates. Points on this grid must have integer coordinates because they represent individual pixels.

concepts.name: Discrete coordinate system
concepts.definition: Discrete coordinate system is a coordinate system where coordinates can only be integer values. This type of system is required when representing points on a pixel grid.

concepts.name: Line rendering
concepts.definition: Line rendering is a common activity within computer graphics that involves drawing lines onto an image. It serves as the fundamental basis for any image rendering process.

concepts.name: Bresenham's line drawing algorithm
concepts.definition: Bresenham's line drawing algorithm is a popular and well-known algorithm used to find the pixels that approximate a line. It achieves this by performing computations using only integer arithmetic to avoid slowing down the computer.

concepts.name: Anti-aliasing operations
concepts.definition: Anti-aliasing operations are additional processes used to remove or reduce the distortion caused by aliasing. These operations ensure a better visual effect for the rendered image.

concepts.name: Graphics library
concepts.definition: A graphics library is an existing implementation that programmers can import into their programming environment. These libraries provide APIs to handle graphics-related concerns and deal with the lower-level tasks involved in computer graphics.

concepts.name: Layered architecture
concepts.definition: Layered architecture is a structural form used to understand the overall virtual reality system, where components are stacked sequentially from top to bottom.

concepts.name: VR application layer
concepts.definition: VR application layer is the highest layer in the layered architecture of the overall virtual reality system. This layer initiates calls to the Software Development Kit (SDK) layer below it.

concepts.name: VR engine
concepts.definition: VR engine is the component responsible for allowing developers to handle graphics using provided APIs without needing direct access to native rendering libraries.

concepts.name: Native rendering library
concepts.definition: Native rendering libraries are low-level components, such as OpenGL or Vulkan, that sit beneath the VR engine. These libraries provide the necessary APIs for the VR engine to execute rendering activities.

concepts.name: Parallelism
concepts.definition: Parallelism is the characteristic of graphics operations where multiple tasks can be performed simultaneously. This ability to process data at the same time allows for a significant gain in performance, which is crucial for real-time rendering.

concepts.name: Multicore system
concepts.definition: A multicore system is a type of hardware that contains a large number of cores or unit processing elements. These cores work together to perform operations simultaneously.

concepts.name: Streaming multiprocessor unit
concepts.definition: A streaming multiprocessor unit is a grouping of cores within a GPU. These cores are capable of performing simple integer and floating-point arithmetic operations.

concepts.name: Rasterization stage
concepts.definition: Rasterization stage determines which pixels on the screen overlap with the device space triangles. This stage exploits inherent parallelism by treating each pixel independently.

concepts.name: Surface texturing
concepts.definition: Surface texturing is a pixel processing activity where the computed color is replaced by the color of a stored texture image. This method applies texture images to the geometry being rendered.

concepts.name: Depth buffer
concepts.definition: Depth buffer is a dedicated memory used by GPUs for hidden surface removal. It stores the distance of the viewer from each pixel in a 3D scene before projection onto a 2D plane.

concepts.name: Navigation technique
concepts.definition: Navigation technique is a method used to move within a specific information point, such as using walking, while other techniques are used to move between points.

concepts.name: Cloud computing
concepts.definition: Cloud computing is a strategy that utilizes the cloud to store large data, such as videos, rather than storing them locally on the client device.

concepts.name: Compression
concepts.definition: Compression is a process used to reduce the storage requirements of data, such as images. This technique allows for the reduction of overall file size.

concepts.name: Unity platform
concepts.definition: Unity platform is a popular and well-known programming environment for developers who wish to work with extended reality systems. It comprises the Unity 3D game engine and a developer's interface that allows a developer to implement ideas.

concepts.name: Unity
concepts.definition: Unity is a cross-platform game engine initially released by Unity Technologies in 2005. It supports both 2D and 3D games or interactive content.

concepts.name: Unity Hub
concepts.definition: Unity Hub is a standalone application that streamlines the way developers find, download, and manage their Unity projects and installations. It allows developers to manage multiple versions of Unity together in one place.

concepts.name: Game Engine
concepts.definition: Game Engine is a middleware that allows developers to build extended reality experiences or systems and deploy them on a specific platform. The engine functions as the underlying component, while the editor interface provides the options for developers to utilize it and build their system.

concepts.name: Editor interface
concepts.definition: Editor interface is the tool where developers utilize different options to build and develop their system. It allows the creation and deployment of realistic immersive environments without requiring mastery of the CG pipeline.

concepts.name: Integrated development environment
concepts.definition: Integrated development environment (IDE) is a tool that provides the developer with all the necessary features required to build and deploy a system. It serves as a comprehensive environment for software creation.

concepts.name: Unity editor interface
concepts.definition: Unity editor interface is a platform used for dealing with extended reality systems, featuring a preference tab that contains XR settings for virtual, mixed, and augmented reality. The interface is composed of several components, including the scene view, game view, hierarchy window, and inspector window.

concepts.name: Scene view
concepts.definition: Scene view is an interactive view of the world that the developer is creating. This view allows the developer to perform selection, manipulation, and modification of the game objects.

concepts.name: Game view
concepts.definition: Game view is the final view of the scene, representing the published or deployed application. The scene is rendered in this view from the camera that the developer has set.

concepts.name: Asset
concepts.definition: Asset is any item that is used within a Unity project to create an application. Assets can represent visual or audio elements, and they may be built internally or imported from outside.

concepts.name: Scene
concepts.definition: Scene is a specific type of asset that contains all or part of a game or application. Developers can create any number of scenes within a project.

concepts.name: Game object
concepts.definition: Game object is a fundamental object that represents elements like characters, props, or scenarios within the scene. It functions as a container that holds components, which then implement the object's specific functionality.

concepts.name: Prefab
concepts.definition: Prefab is a template used to create, configure, and store game objects. Prefabs allow users to make multiple instances of a specific object type within the game scene.

concepts.name: Component
concepts.definition: Component is a functional module that implements specific behaviors and capabilities for an object. Game objects act as the container that holds and organizes these components.

concepts.name: Unity developer environment
concepts.definition: Unity developer environment is an implementation platform that includes an editor interface allowing a developer to create, build, and deploy a system. This interface provides the necessary support for building an XR experience.

concepts.name: Render pipeline support
concepts.definition: Render pipeline support is the graphics support offered by Unity that allows the implementation of the entire pipeline. This support ensures that a developer does not need to worry too much about how to implement the pipeline stages.

concepts.name: Built-in render pipeline
concepts.definition: Built-in render pipeline is one of the three pre-built render pipelines provided by Unity. This pipeline has limited options for customization, requiring the user to work with the existing features.

concepts.name: Universal Render Pipeline
concepts.definition: Universal Render Pipeline (URP) is a customizable pipeline that allows the creation of optimized graphics across a wide range of platforms. This pipeline handles many stages of optimization internally, minimizing the developer's effort.

concepts.name: High definition render pipeline
concepts.definition: High definition render pipeline (HDRP) is a customizable pipeline designed to create cutting-edge, high-fidelity graphics. This pipeline is specifically meant for photorealistic implementation and is typically used on high-end platforms.

concepts.name: Material
concepts.definition: A material describes the appearance of a surface, dictating how that surface should be rendered. Materials encode information such as color tints, tiling details, and references to textures.

concepts.name: Texture
concepts.definition: A texture is a bitmap image that is applied over the surface of a mesh. Textures function as a method to assign colors and represent surface properties like reflectivity and roughness.

concepts.name: Model
concepts.definition: A model is a file that contains data detailing the shape and appearance of a three-dimensional object. These files serve as the object representation within the graphics pipeline.

concepts.name: 3D mesh
concepts.definition: A 3D mesh is the primary graphics primitive used in Unity. These meshes can be either triangulated or quadrangulated polygonal shapes.

concepts.name: Skybox
concepts.definition: Skybox is a cube with different textures on its faces, which creates the feeling of a 360-degree environment. This allows the user to see different things as they move their head.

concepts.name: Halo effect
concepts.definition: Halo effect is a visual effect that creates light areas surrounding light sources. Typically, this effect is used to give the impression of small dust particles in the air.

concepts.name: Lens flare effect
concepts.definition: Lens flare effect simulates the effect of lights refracting inside a camera lens.

concepts.name: Line renderer effect
concepts.definition: Line renderer effect is a visual effect that draws a straight line between an array of two or more points in 3D space. This effect can be used to draw anything from a simple line to a complex spiral.

concepts.name: Middleware game engine
concepts.definition: Middleware game engine is the layer in the XR system architecture, such as Unity, that utilizes native rendering libraries. This engine sits between the software development kits and the operating system.

concepts.name: AutoGraphics API
concepts.definition: AutoGraphics API is a feature that, when checked in player settings, includes a set of built-in graphics APIs. This feature uses the appropriate API at runtime to produce the best-case scenario for the platform.

concepts.name: Rigid body
concepts.definition: Rigid body is a property that, when attached to a game object, allows that object to respond to gravity. This enables movement, such as falling or bouncing, to appear realistic and consistent with everyday experience.

concepts.name: Collider
concepts.definition: Collider defines the shape of a game object specifically for the purpose of physical collisions. Collider allows the system to manage objects or object shapes after they interact with other objects.

concepts.name: Joint
concepts.definition: Joint connects a rigid body to another rigid body or to a fixed point in space. Joints can apply forces to move rigid bodies, and joint limits can be used to restrict that movement.

concepts.name: Physics articulation
concepts.definition: Physics articulation provides a realistic physics behavior that involves joints. Physics articulation describes how an overall structure, comprising multiple joints, moves as a whole.

concepts.name: Humanoid animation retargeting
concepts.definition: Humanoid animation retargeting is the ability to apply animations from one character model onto another. This feature allows for the reuse of animation data across different character designs.

concepts.name: Audio listener
concepts.definition: Audio listener is a component that listens to all audio playing in the scene and transfers it to the computer speakers. It functions as the internal ears of the game, determining the spatial relationship of all heard audio.

concepts.name: Audio filter
concepts.definition: Audio filter is a component that modifies the output of an audio source after it has been generated. These components allow developers to modify the audio option and generate various sound effects.

concepts.name: Scripting support
concepts.definition: Scripting support is a crucial programming support provided by the Unity Development Environment. It allows a programmer to customize the experience by writing scripts or small pieces of code.

concepts.name: Script
concepts.definition: Script is a new type of component that a developer creates to attach to a game object, allowing it to behave according to the developer's design.

concepts.name: Start function
concepts.definition: Start function is a function that serves as the starting point of the script. This function is called whenever the script is executed.

concepts.name: Update function
concepts.definition: Update function is a function that is invoked in each frame. This function is called whenever the script executes and a change happens.

concepts.name: Vector3
concepts.definition: Vector3 is a data type used to represent the position of a 3D point. This data type captures three coordinates within the vector.

concepts.name: Debug.Log function
concepts.definition: Debug.Log function is a construct that prints a message onto the console output. This allows the user to see the script's execution results.

concepts.name: Destroy function
concepts.definition: Destroy function is a method that can be attached to a game object to specify a time after which that object should be removed from the scene. This function allows the object to be destroyed after a specified duration, typically measured in seconds.

concepts.name: Event function
concepts.definition: Event functions are a class of functions activated by Unity in response to specific events that occur during gameplay. These functions allow developers to implement behaviors, such as physical reactions or interactive responses, when predefined conditions like collisions, updates, or mouse clicks are met.

concepts.name: Parameters
concepts.definition: Parameters are inputs that are given to a function each time that function is called. Functions may or may not require these inputs, depending on the specific task they are designed to perform.

concepts.name: Event handler
concepts.definition: Event handler is the function that receives control when a specific event occurs, executing its body before passing control back to the main programming environment.

concepts.name: Instantiating prefab at runtime
concepts.definition: Instantiating prefab at runtime is the process of dynamically creating a prefab object during execution, which requires the writing script to maintain a reference to that prefab.

concepts.name: Entry-controlled loop
concepts.definition: Entry-controlled loops, such as for or while, check the loop condition before the loop body executes, meaning the body may never run if the initial condition is false.

concepts.name: Exit-controlled loop
concepts.definition: Exit-controlled loops, such as do while, execute the loop body at least one time because the testing condition is checked only after the body has completed its execution.

concepts.name: Transform property
concepts.definition: Transform property is a property attached to every game object in a scene. Transform property stores and allows manipulation of an object's position, rotation, and scale.

concepts.name: Coroutine
concepts.definition: Coroutine is a method that allows a developer to pause execution and return control to the game engine. Coroutine then continues its execution from where it left off during the following frame.

concepts.name: InvokeRepeating
concepts.definition: InvokeRepeating is a function that calls a specified method at a specific time. InvokeRepeating then repeatedly calls that method at every specified interval.

concepts.name: Scripting
concepts.definition: Scripting is a method used for developing a customized experience. This process involves a higher degree of programming compared to creating a basic system.

concepts.name: Image target
concepts.definition: Image target is the specific image asset used in a marker-based AR application that the Vuforia engine attempts to recognize. This image is captured and placed within the asset folder for the project.

concepts.name: Device-specific SDK
concepts.definition: Device-specific SDKs are tools utilized to enable various devices to access unique data, sensory data, or input data. These kits allow developers to integrate device-specific functionalities into their systems.
